records.name: Developmental Disabilities Resource Center (DDRC): Community Centered Board
records.description: Designated Community Centered Board for Jefferson, Clear Creek, Gilpin and Summit counties. It determines developmental disability eligibility and funding routes for children and adults. Case management for the Medicaid waivers in Jefferson and Clear Creek counties moved to Jefferson County Human Services in 2024.
records.next_step: Call DDRC to ask about a developmental disability determination, and ask who provides case management in your county now.
constraints: Eligibility is for qualifying developmental disabilities.
records.phone_note: DDRC main line, from the state case management directory

records.name: Developmental Pathways: Community Centered Board and case management agency
records.description: Community Centered Board for Arapahoe and Douglas counties and the part of Adams County inside Aurora city limits. It determines eligibility and provides programs for people with developmental disabilities, and serves as a case management agency for the HCBS waivers.
records.next_step: Call and ask for an intake coordinator to start an eligibility determination.
constraints: In Adams County this covers only the city of Aurora.
records.phone_note: Case management agency line, from the state directory

records.name: Imagine!: direct services provider for Boulder and Broomfield
records.description: Imagine! provides direct services for people with developmental disabilities, including adult day services, school-age programs and residential services. Since July 1, 2024, case management and waiver intake for Boulder, Broomfield and Gilpin counties are handled by A&I Avenues, which is a separate agency.
records.next_step: Call A&I Avenues about waiver funding and eligibility, and Imagine! about services.

records.name: Colorado Community Centered Boards and case management agencies (statewide directory)
records.org: Colorado Department of Health Care Policy & Financing
records.description: Colorado has one case management agency (CMA) for each of 20 service areas, and these agencies handle intake, eligibility and case management for the developmental disability waivers. Community Centered Boards still provide services. The state directory lists the agency and phone for each county.
records.next_step: Find your county in the directory, then call the case management agency listed for it.

records.name: Michigan Community Mental Health Services Programs (CMHSPs)
records.org: Michigan Department of Health and Human Services
records.description: Specialty behavioral health services for people with developmental disabilities are delivered through county-based Community Mental Health Services Programs. Each county has a CMHSP (some serve several counties) that handles intake and service planning.
records.next_step: Use the state CMHSP list to find the program for your county, then call and ask for developmental disability services intake.

records.name: Utah Division of Services for People with Disabilities (DSPD)
records.org: Utah Department of Health & Human Services
records.description: State division that oversees home and community-based services for Utahns with disabilities. Call the intake line to ask about eligibility, the waiting list and services.
records.next_step: Call 1-844-ASK-DSPD and ask about eligibility and how to apply for services.
constraints: Eligibility is for qualifying disabilities and there can be a waiting list.
records.phone_note: Toll-free intake line; administrative office 801-538-4200

records.name: Illinois developmental disability services: find your ISC agency
records.org: Illinois Department of Human Services, Division of Developmental Disabilities
records.description: In Illinois the first step is to meet your regional Independent Service Coordination (ISC) agency, which registers you in the PUNS waiting list database. The state office locator finds your agency by county.
records.next_step: Search the DHS Office Locator with Office Type set to Developmental Disability Services, or call the hotline, then ask the ISC agency to register you in PUNS.
constraints: Waiver funding is offered from the PUNS list as it becomes available.
records.phone_note: Division of Developmental Disabilities hotline (1-888-DD-PLANS)

records.name: Arizona Division of Developmental Disabilities (DDD)
records.description: State division that provides supports and services for eligible Arizonans with developmental disabilities, through district and local offices. Eligibility offices are in Flagstaff (North), Chandler (East), Tucson (South) and Phoenix (Central).

records.name: Maine adult developmental services: intake and eligibility (3 regional offices)
records.org: Maine Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Aging and Disability Services
records.description: To apply for adult developmental disability services, apply for MaineCare if you do not have it, complete the application packet with a comprehensive evaluation and adaptive behavior scale, and send it to intake. An intake coordinator contacts you within ten days. Eligible people get a list of case management agencies. Regional intake offices: Lewiston 207-795-4664, Augusta 207-624-8068 and Bangor 207-561-4380.
records.next_step: Call the regional intake supervisor, or email your completed application packet.
constraints: Adults 18 and older with an intellectual disability or autism that began before age 22.
records.phone_note: Augusta regional office; Lewiston 207-795-4664, Bangor 207-561-4380

records.name: Rhode Island Division of Developmental Disabilities: eligibility and application (statewide)
records.org: Rhode Island Department of Behavioral Healthcare, Developmental Disabilities and Hospitals
records.description: You apply to the Division of Developmental Disabilities for adult services. Students can apply 2 months before their 17th birthday, and a decision comes within 30 days of a complete application. You also need Medicaid eligibility to start services. The Rhode Island Parent Information Network can help you fill out the application at 401-270-0101.
records.next_step: Call the Eligibility Unit to get an application or ask questions.
constraints: Adults 18 and older with an intellectual or developmental disability diagnosed before age 22.
records.phone_note: Eligibility Unit, Cranston; Spanish line 401-462-3014

records.name: Minnesota Developmental Disabilities Waiver: apply through your county or tribal nation (statewide)
records.description: Minnesota runs its Developmental Disabilities (DD) Waiver through county and tribal nation "lead agencies." You apply at the county social services office or tribal nation where you live, and a screening decides eligibility. The state lists a DD waiver contact for each lead agency.
records.next_step: Call Disability Hub MN or your county social services office and ask how to apply for the DD waiver.
constraints: People with a developmental disability or related condition who need the level of care of an intermediate care facility.
records.phone_note: Disability Hub MN, Monday to Friday 8:30 am to 5 pm; or call your county social services office

records.name: Alaska Developmental Disabilities Resource Connection (DDRC) and ADRC: where to start for waivers (statewide)
records.org: Alaska Department of Health, Division of Senior and Disabilities Services
records.description: The DDRC is the first stop for Alaskans with an intellectual or developmental disability and their families. DDRC staff can help you get on the waiting list (the DD Registry) for the IDD and Individualized Supports waivers. An Aging and Disability Resource Center (ADRC) can refer you to a DDRC. After you are drawn from the list, a care coordinator helps you apply.
records.next_step: Call the ADRC and DDRC toll-free line and ask to start intake.
constraints: You must qualify for Medicaid and meet an intermediate care facility level of care for the IDD and Individualized Supports waivers.
records.phone_note: ADRC and DDRC toll-free; Division of Senior and Disabilities Services in Anchorage 907-269-3666 or 800-478-9996

records.name: Wisconsin programs for adults with developmental and intellectual disabilities (statewide)
records.description: Wisconsin offers several long-term care programs for adults with intellectual or developmental disabilities, including Family Care and IRIS, the self-directed option. You enroll through your local Aging and Disability Resource Center (ADRC) or tribal aging and disability resource specialist. They complete a functional screen and help with the Medicaid application.
records.next_step: Contact your local ADRC and ask to start the long-term care functional screen.
constraints: Adults 18 and older who need long-term care and are eligible for Medicaid.
records.phone_note: Find your local ADRC through the state page

records.name: Wisconsin Children's Long-Term Support program: apply through your county (statewide)
records.description: The Children's Long-Term Support program serves children with disabilities, including developmental disabilities. You start by contacting your county health and human services agency. A support and service coordinator visits your home, uses an online tool to look at your child's care needs, and helps with enrollment.
records.next_step: Call your county health and human services agency and say you want services for your child.
constraints: Children with disabilities who meet the program's eligibility rules.
records.phone_note: Use your county health and human services number

records.name: Disability Hub MN (free statewide help line)
records.org: Minnesota Department of Human Services, delivered by the Metropolitan and Southeastern Minnesota Centers for Independent Living
records.description: A free statewide service for people with disabilities, including developmental disabilities, and the people who support them. Options counselors explain benefits and health coverage, help with forms and applications, and point you to waiver programs and local services. It also runs Disability Benefits 101 and Housing Benefits 101.
records.next_step: Call or chat with a Hub expert, Monday to Friday, 8:30 am to 5 pm.
constraints: Free; serves all languages.
records.phone_note: Monday to Friday, 8:30 am to 5 pm

records.description: Washington Traumatic Brain Injury Council is run by or through Washington Department of Social and Health Services, which the National Association of State Head Injury Administrators lists as the state lead on brain injury. State brain injury programs coordinate services, trust fund or waiver supports, public information and the state advisory council for people with traumatic or acquired brain injury, including veterans and people hurt in crashes, falls or sports. The statewide advocacy group is the Brain Northwest.
records.next_step: Contact the program and ask about brain injury resource facilitation, any trust fund or waiver services you may qualify for, and local support groups.
constraints: Services and eligibility vary a lot by state; many are funded by trust funds or Medicaid waivers with limited slots.

records.name: USDA Rural Development home repair loans and grants (Alabama)
records.org: USDA Rural Development, Montgomery state office
records.description: The USDA Section 504 Home Repair program gives loans to low-income and very-low-income homeowners in eligible rural areas to repair, improve or modernize their homes, and grants to very-low-income homeowners age 62 and older to remove health and safety hazards. Repairs and improvements can sometimes include accessibility changes such as ramps or bathroom work, so ask the local office what qualifies.
records.next_step: Call the Alabama Rural Development state office, ask for Single Family Housing, and ask which local office takes 504 repair applications for your county.
constraints: Homeowners only; the home must be in an eligible rural area and household income must be low or very low for the county.
Grants are for homeowners age 62 and older with very low income; funding is limited each federal fiscal year.
records.phone_note: State office main line from the USDA Rural Development state office directory; confirm before calling

records.name: Alabama State Long-Term Care Ombudsman
records.description: Every state has an Office of the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman. Ombudsmen are free, confidential advocates for people living in nursing homes, assisted living and other care facilities. They take complaints about care, rights, discharge and billing and work to resolve them at the resident's direction. Family members, friends and visiting volunteers can call too.
records.next_step: Call the state ombudsman office and ask to be connected to the local ombudsman for the facility where the resident lives.
constraints: The ombudsman works for the resident and cannot take sides with the facility or family; services are free and confidential.

records.name: Eldercare Locator (Administration for Community Living)
records.org: Administration for Community Living, operated by USAging
records.description: The Eldercare Locator is a free national call center and website from the U.S. Administration for Community Living. It connects older adults, people with disabilities and their caregivers to the local Area Agency on Aging, the state unit on aging, and the nearest long-term care ombudsman. Call or text with a zip code or city and state.
records.next_step: Call or text 1-800-677-1116 and ask for your Area Agency on Aging, home modification help, transportation, or the long-term care ombudsman for a facility.
constraints: Information and referral only; services come from the local agencies it connects you to.
records.phone_note: National line; confirm before calling

records.name: ADA paratransit: your rights and who to call (FTA Office of Civil Rights)
records.org: Federal Transit Administration, Office of Civil Rights
records.description: Public transit systems that run regular bus or rail routes must also provide ADA complementary paratransit for people who cannot use those routes because of a disability. Service must be origin to destination, run the same days and hours as the routes, and cost no more than twice the regular fare. Eligibility is based on your functional ability to use the fixed-route system, not on a diagnosis. Call your local transit agency to apply; call the FTA Office of Civil Rights if you are denied or have a complaint.
records.next_step: Call your local transit agency and ask for its ADA paratransit application. If you are denied or have problems, call the FTA Office of Civil Rights at 888-446-4511.
constraints: Paratransit is only required near fixed bus or rail routes (generally within three-quarters of a mile) and only during the same hours the routes run.
Rural dial-a-ride and demand-response services for the general public are not covered by the ADA paratransit rule.
records.phone_note: National line; confirm before calling

records.org: New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services, Bureau of Elderly and Adult Services
records.description: Medicaid home and community-based waiver run by the state aging bureau. HomeMods.org lists it as covering home modifications and repairs for older adults and adults with chronic illness.
records.next_step: Ask NHCarePath or the aging bureau how to apply, then ask your care coordinator whether a ramp, bathroom or entry change can go in your care plan.
constraints: Medicaid financial and level-of-care rules apply.
records.phone_note: No phone is printed in the HomeMods.org listing; use the website to find the current number.

The state passes the money to eligible nonprofits, public agencies and transit operators, which run the vehicles and rides.
records.next_step: If you need a ride, ask your Area Agency on Aging, Center for Independent Living or local transit agency which 5310-funded rides serve your county. If you run a nonprofit or transit service, use this page to see how and when to apply.
constraints: Funds go to eligible organizations, so riders use the services those groups run rather than applying for money themselves.
Application rounds, deadlines and forms change; check the page for the current cycle.
records.phone_note: No phone is printed in the National RTAP list; use the state page to find the current contact.

records.name: Section 5310 and the RIde program (Rhode Island)
records.description: Rhode Island has one statewide transit agency, RIPTA, which receives and administers the Section 5310 money. Its state management plan says the sole priority for these funds is capital purchases for the RIde program, which provides transportation for seniors and people with disabilities.
records.next_step: Call RIPTA and ask about RIde eligibility and how to apply for a ride.
constraints: Funding is used for the RIde program rather than passed to a competitive grant round, according to the state management plan.
records.phone_note: No phone is printed in the source document; use the RIPTA website to find the current number.

records.name: Section 5310 vehicle program for organizations serving seniors and people with disabilities (District of Columbia)
records.description: DDOT administers the federal Section 5310 program for the District. Its management plan describes providing federally funded vehicles to eligible organizations that serve older adults and people with disabilities.
records.next_step: If you run an eligible nonprofit, ask DDOT for the current Section 5310 forms and application dates. If you need a ride, ask your Area Agency on Aging or the DC Office on Aging.
constraints: Vehicles go to eligible organizations, not to individuals.
records.phone_note: No phone is printed in the DDOT page; use the DDOT website to find the current contact.

records.name: Medicaid rides to medical appointments (AL)
records.org: State Medicaid agency and its ride contractors
records.description: Medicaid pays for rides to covered medical appointments for members who have no other way to get there. A 2024 report from the federal transportation coordination council says Alabama runs rides directly through 10 regional NEMT districts (information collected Sep 2024).
records.next_step: Call the member services number on your Medicaid card and ask how to schedule a ride, how far ahead to book, and whether wheelchair-accessible vehicles are available.
constraints: Rides are for Medicaid-covered services; who runs scheduling depends on your health plan and county.
The contractors named were current in 2024 and change often, so confirm with your plan or the state Medicaid office.
records.phone_note: No phone is printed in the report; the member services number on your Medicaid card can connect you to ride scheduling.

records.next_step: If you need a ride, ask your Area Agency on Aging, Center for Independent Living or regional transit provider which 5310-funded rides serve your town. If you run a nonprofit or transit service, ask MaineDOT's transit staff how and when to apply.
constraints: Funds go to eligible organizations, so riders use the services those groups run rather than applying for money themselves.
The link goes to MaineDOT's 2024 state management plan rather than a program landing page; application dates are set by MaineDOT.
records.phone_note: No program phone is printed in the plan; use the MaineDOT transit website to find the current contact.

records.description: Advocates provide legal support, advocacy and information to people with disabilities who receive SSI or SSDI and have a disability-related employment issue. records.description: Services for the Blind and Physically Handicapped (Parkersburg and Wood County Public Library) in Parkersburg is part of the Library of Congress National Library Service for the Blind and Print Disabled (NLS) network. The NLS Find a Library directory lists it as a subregional library serving Calhoun, Jackson, Pleasants, Ritchie, Roane, Tyler, Wirt and Wood counties. Network libraries supply audio and braille reading materials to people who cannot read standard print.
records.next_step: Call 304-420-4587, say you want to apply for talking-book service, and ask about eligibility, how to get a playback device and how to download books.
constraints: The network serves people who are blind or print disabled; ask the library what proof of eligibility it needs.
Service areas and hours change; confirm with the library before you rely on this listing.
records.phone_note: Main line as listed in the Library of Congress NLS Find a Library directory; library website as listed: parkwoodlib.com

records.name: iCanConnect in Alabama: free phone and internet equipment for people who are deaf-blind
records.org: iCanConnect (National Deaf-Blind Equipment Distribution Program), Alabama program
records.description: iCanConnect provides free distance communication technology and training to people with both significant hearing and vision loss. The FCC administers it and a local partner carries it out in each state, including Alabama. The Alabama page on iCanConnect.org gives the local contact.
records.next_step: Open the Alabama page for the local program's phone, email and mailing instructions, or call the national iCanConnect line and ask to be connected. Ask who can verify your hearing and vision loss and what income documents are needed.
constraints: For low-income people who are deaf-blind (combined hearing and vision loss); programs verify disability and income.
Contact details and the local partner can change; use the state page for the current contact.
records.phone_note: National iCanConnect line; the Alabama page lists the local program contact

records.name: ADA Information Line (U.S. Department of Justice): questions about disability rights law
records.org: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Rights Division, Disability Rights Section
records.description: The Justice Department's ADA Information Line answers questions about the Americans with Disabilities Act, including what businesses and state and local governments must do for people with disabilities. ADA.gov also has guidance, fact sheets and how to report a violation.
records.next_step: Call the line or open ADA.gov, say what happened (for example a business refusing access, a missing ramp or a denied accommodation), and ask which ADA section covers it and how to file a complaint.
constraints: It gives information about the law; it is not a lawyer and does not represent you.
Check ADA.gov for the current hours.
records.phone_note: TTY 833-610-1264; weekday hours are on ADA.gov

records.name: File a disability rights complaint with the Department of Justice (ADA)
records.org: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Rights Division
records.description: ADA.gov has a page for filing a disability rights violation complaint with the Justice Department, for example about a business, a state or local government service, or a building that is not accessible.
records.next_step: Open the complaint page, describe what happened, where and when, and what you asked for. Keep copies of letters, photos and names. Call the ADA Information Line if you are unsure whether the ADA covers your situation.
constraints: A complaint is not the same as a lawsuit and does not guarantee an investigation or a remedy.
Your state Protection and Advocacy agency can help you decide how to proceed.
records.phone_note: ADA Information Line; TTY 833-610-1264

records.name: Service animals and the ADA: what businesses and governments may ask
records.org: U.S. Department of Justice, Civil Rights Division, Disability Rights Section
records.description: Justice Department guidance says that under the ADA only dogs are recognized as service animals in businesses and in state and local government services, with a separate provision for miniature horses. When it is not obvious what a service animal does, staff may ask two questions: whether the dog is required because of a disability, and what work or task it has been trained to perform. The guidance notes that some state and local laws, and other federal laws such as the Fair Housing Act and the Air Carrier Access Act, define service animals more broadly.
records.next_step: Read the ADA.gov service animal questions and answers, then call the ADA Information Line if a business or agency turned you away. For housing or air travel, ask which rule applies.
constraints: Rules differ for housing and air travel; ask before you rely on the ADA answer there.
State and local laws may add protections.
Staff may not ask for documentation, ask the dog to demonstrate its task, or ask about your disability. Online certificates and registrations give no rights under the ADA.
A business may ask that the dog be removed if it is out of control or not housebroken.
records.phone_note: ADA Information Line; TTY 833-610-1264

records.name: DOT disability hotline for air travelers: wheelchair damage, boarding and other airline problems
records.org: U.S. Department of Transportation, Aviation Consumer Protection Division
records.description: The Department of Transportation runs a toll-free hotline for air travelers with disabilities who have a service problem that needs help in real time. DOT says to ask for the airline's Complaint Resolution Official first, and to call the hotline when a complaint is beyond that official's control. To have DOT investigate, you send a complaint by online form or by mail.
records.next_step: Ask for the airline's Complaint Resolution Official at the airport, then call the hotline if the problem is not fixed. After a trip, file a written or online complaint and keep your photos, repair estimates and receipts.
constraints: Reported rule: airlines must repair or replace a wheelchair or assistive device they damage or lose on covered flights; confirm current rules with DOT before you rely on this.
Hotline hours are weekdays 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern except federal holidays.
records.phone_note: Weekdays 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern; if you are deaf, hard of hearing or have a speech disability, dial 7-1-1 for relay

records.name: TSA Cares: airport security screening help for travelers with disabilities
records.description: The DOT travel brochure says travelers can call TSA Cares before arriving at the airport to discuss questions or concerns about security screening, including when traveling with a wheelchair or other assistive device.
records.next_step: Call TSA Cares a few days before your flight, describe your device and any medical needs, and ask what to expect at screening.
constraints: Hours are not listed in the source; confirm them when you call.
records.phone_note: Listed in the DOT ABCs of Accessible Travel brochure

records.name: America the Beautiful Access Pass: free lifetime pass to national parks and federal recreation lands
records.org: National Park Service and federal recreation agencies
records.description: The Access Pass is free for U.S. citizens or residents of any age who have a medically determined permanent disability that severely limits one or more major life activities; it does not have to be a 100 percent disability. You can pick up a physical pass in person at more than 1,000 federal recreation sites, order one by mail through the USGS Online Store, or get a digital pass from Recreation.gov.
records.next_step: Bring a photo ID plus proof of a permanent disability: a signed letter from a licensed physician, a federal agency document such as VA or Social Security disability benefits, or a state agency document such as vocational rehabilitation. Apply at a federal recreation site for the fastest result.
constraints: Mail orders can take up to three weeks, and an order receipt cannot substitute for the pass.
Online and mail orders may carry a processing fee; the pass itself is free for eligible people.
records.phone_note: The NPS page lists no phone; its Contact Us page and the USGS Store FAQ handle questions

records.name: Move United: find a local adaptive sports and recreation program
records.description: Move United is a national nonprofit established in 1956 that works with 259 member organizations in 45 states to give people of all abilities access to sports and recreation. Its site has a nearest-location finder for member organizations, an events list, and pages on adaptive equipment, youth and adult programs, and grants.
records.next_step: Open the location finder, choose your area, and call the nearest member organization to ask about sports offered, trial sessions and whether equipment is available to borrow.
constraints: The site lists no program fees; costs, equipment loans and eligibility are set by each local member organization, so ask.
records.phone_note: Move United national office, Rockville, Maryland

records.name: HUD fair housing complaint and hotline: denied accommodation or modification (ramps, rails, accessible parking)
records.org: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity
records.description: HUD takes housing discrimination complaints, including when a landlord or housing provider refuses a reasonable accommodation or modification for a disability. HUD guidance gives examples such as allowing a service animal or providing an accessible parking space. HUD also says it is illegal for a housing provider to act against you because you filed a complaint.
records.next_step: Write down what you asked for and how the provider answered, keep copies, and say how the change connects to your disability. Then report it on the HUD page or call the hotline, or contact a local fair housing center.
constraints: Complaints to HUD are generally filed within one year of the discrimination; confirm the deadline with HUD.
In private housing the tenant may have to pay for a requested modification such as a ramp, while the landlord pays for an accommodation; ask HUD or a fair housing center about your case.
records.phone_note: HUD National Discrimination Hotline, English and Spanish; Federal Relay 800-877-8339 (TTY 800-927-9275 is also published)

records.name: Medicare equipment problems: repairs, rental supplier duties and replacement after a disaster
records.description: The official Medicare booklet on durable medical equipment says that if you own your equipment, the supplier that sold it is not required to repair it, and you can look for a supplier that can maintain or repair it on the Medicare site. If you rent equipment, the supplier must maintain and repair it, answer your calls, and service, repair or replace it when needed. If Original Medicare already paid for equipment such as a wheelchair or walker that was damaged or lost in an emergency or disaster, Medicare will in most cases cover the cost to repair or replace it.
records.next_step: Call 1-800-MEDICARE, say whether you own or rent the equipment and what is broken, and ask for suppliers that can repair it. If a rental supplier will not answer or fix it, ask Medicare how to report that.
constraints: Applies to Original Medicare; if you have a Medicare Advantage plan, ask the plan about its supplier and coverage rules.
Coverage rules, prior authorization and replacement limits change; confirm on Medicare.gov before you rely on this.

records.name: Medicare Rights Center helpline: denials and suppliers who will not repair or replace equipment
records.description: The Medicare Rights Center runs a national consumer helpline. Its advocacy toolkit says more than 500 clients a year contact it about getting durable medical equipment, including coverage denials and suppliers who refuse to repair or replace broken equipment.
records.next_step: Call the helpline with your Medicare details and the equipment problem, and ask what appeal or complaint step fits your situation.
constraints: It gives guidance and advocacy support; it does not provide or repair equipment.
records.phone_note: National consumer helpline

records.name: State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP): free local Medicare counseling
records.description: Every state has a SHIP that can explain Medicare coverage of durable medical equipment and other benefits. The national SHIP site lists a toll-free number and a state-by-state locator.
records.next_step: Call the national number or open the SHIP site, choose your state, and ask a counselor how Medicare covers the equipment you need or a denial you received.
constraints: Counseling is about Medicare coverage and plans; it is not a source of equipment funding.
records.phone_note: National SHIP number as listed by the National Council on Aging

records.name: Light Upon Light: disability-inclusion education, advocacy and mentorship (Everett)
records.description: Washington 501(c)(3) nonprofit based in Everett and led by a differently abled founder. It works through advocacy, accessibility, education and equality to build a community where dignity is honored and belonging is expected. Its website also has pages for donating and volunteering.
records.next_step: Call or email, or open the website to see the Programs page and ask how to take part or bring disability-inclusion education to your group.
constraints: Listing built from the organization’s own website (programs are on its Programs page) and its public Idealist profile for the Everett location; confirm current programs and contact details with the organization.
records.phone_note: Phone number published on the organization’s website

records.name: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline: call, text or chat, any time
records.description: Free, confidential support for people in emotional distress or crisis. The Lifeline says it is available 24 hours a day, every day of the year.
records.next_step: Call or text 988, or open the chat on the website. If you are Deaf or hard of hearing, call 988 from your videophone for ASL, text 988, or dial 711 and then 988.
constraints: Text and chat are also offered in Spanish.
In immediate danger, call 911.
records.phone_note: Call or text. Chat: chat.988lifeline.org

records.name: 911 and Text-to-911: reaching emergency help when you cannot make a voice call
records.description: In an emergency, the FCC says to make a voice call to 911 if you can, because a call gives the 911 center more information. Texting 911 works only in certain areas. If you text 911 where it is not available, your phone company must send back an automatic message telling you to reach 911 another way.
records.next_step: If you are deaf, hard of hearing or have a speech disability and text-to-911 is not available where you are, the FCC says to use a TTY or a relay service if possible. The FCC keeps a list of areas that accept texts; check yours before you need it.
constraints: Each 911 call center decides whether to accept texts.
records.phone_note: Make a voice call if you can

records.name: Crisis Text Line: text HOME to 741741
records.description: Free, confidential crisis support by text message, 24 hours a day, from anywhere in the United States. A live volunteer crisis counselor answers.
records.next_step: Text HOME to 741741. For Spanish, text HOLA to 741741. You can also start a chat from the website.
constraints: Message and data rates may apply.
In immediate danger, call 911.
records.contact_how: Text HOME to 741741 (Spanish: text HOLA). No voice call is needed.

records.name: Veterans Crisis Line: dial 988, then press 1
records.description: Free, confidential crisis support from the Veterans Crisis Line, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year.
records.next_step: Dial 988 and press 1, text 838255, or chat online from the website.
constraints: In immediate danger, call 911.
records.phone_note: Then press 1. Text: 838255

records.name: National Domestic Violence Hotline
records.description: Live advocates answer by phone, text and online chat 24 hours a day, every day of the year.
records.next_step: Call 1-800-799-7233, text START to 88788, or use the chat on the website. Deaf callers can use The Deaf Hotline, listed next, for help in ASL.
constraints: In immediate danger, call 911.
records.phone_note: 1-800-799-SAFE. Text START to 88788

records.name: The Deaf Hotline: 24-hour ASL help for relationship abuse
records.org: ADWAS, in partnership with the National Domestic Violence Hotline
records.description: A free, confidential ASL hotline, open 24 hours a day, for Deaf survivors of relationship abuse.
records.next_step: Call 855-812-1001 by videophone, or use the contact form on the website.
constraints: In immediate danger, call 911.
records.phone_note: ASL videophone line

records.name: Adult Protective Services: report abuse, neglect or exploitation of an adult with a disability
records.org: National Adult Protective Services Association directory and the Eldercare Locator
records.description: Every state has an Adult Protective Services program that takes and looks into reports that an older adult or an adult with a disability is being abused, neglected or financially exploited. Anyone can make a report, and you can make one without giving your name. Choose a state in this directory to see its reporting line.
records.next_step: Choose your state above to see its reporting line, or call the Eldercare Locator and ask how to report where you live. Say who is at risk, where they are and what you have seen or been told.
constraints: In about half the states Adult Protective Services also looks into abuse in nursing homes and other care facilities; elsewhere a different office does.
In immediate danger, call 911.
records.phone_note: Eldercare Locator, Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. Eastern

records.name: Disaster Distress Helpline: call or text 1-800-985-5990
records.org: SAMHSA (Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration)
records.description: A national helpline for people in distress because of a disaster. SAMHSA says it is available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, to all residents of the United States and its territories.
records.next_step: Call or text 1-800-985-5990 and say what happened and how you are doing.
constraints: In immediate danger, call 911.
records.phone_note: Call or text

records.name: Disability & Disaster Hotline
records.org: The Partnership for Inclusive Disaster Strategies
records.description: A hotline led by disabled people, for disabled people, before, during and after disasters and emergencies. It gives information, referrals and guidance on urgent disability-related needs, FEMA and other disaster programs, accessible transportation, shelter and temporary housing, health care access and disability accommodations.
records.next_step: Call or text 1-800-626-4959, or email, and say what you need. The hotline takes messages at any hour and says it intends to respond to all callers within 24 hours.
constraints: Because a reply can take up to a day, call 911 if you are in immediate danger.
Videophone for Deaf callers and information in other languages are available on request.
records.phone_note: Call or text

records.name: SAMHSA National Helpline: find mental health or substance use treatment
records.org: SAMHSA (Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration)
records.description: A free, confidential treatment referral and information service for people and families facing mental health or substance use conditions. It is open 24 hours a day, every day of the year, in English and Spanish.
records.next_step: Call and say what kind of help you are looking for and where you live. Ask for treatment programs and support groups near you.
constraints: For a crisis, call or text 988.

records.name: NAMI HelpLine: information and peer support for mental health conditions
records.description: A free peer-support service that gives information, resource referrals and support to people living with a mental health condition, their family members and caregivers. It is open Monday to Friday, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. Eastern.
records.next_step: Call 1-800-950-6264, text NAMI to 62640, or email. Ask about support groups and how to reach your local NAMI affiliate.
constraints: NAMI says the HelpLine is not a hotline, crisis line or suicide prevention line. In a crisis, call or text 988.
Closed on federal holidays.
records.phone_note: 1-800-950-NAMI. Text NAMI to 62640

records.name: 211: one call for local help with food, housing, bills and more
records.description: 211 connects you to local help. United Way’s 211 site lists help with paying bills, food, housing and utility costs, disaster recovery, health care costs, mental health and substance use, and says every call is confidential.
records.next_step: Dial 211 and say what you need and your ZIP code. If 211 does not connect from your phone, use the website to find your local 211.
constraints: Each local 211 is run separately, so hours and services differ.

records.name: DIAL: federal database of local disability organizations in every state and territory
records.description: A searchable federal database of state and local organizations that help people with disabilities live independently. It lists Centers for Independent Living, Protection and Advocacy agencies, Assistive Technology Act programs, University Centers for Excellence in Developmental Disabilities and State Developmental Disabilities Councils, including those in the U.S. territories and the Protection and Advocacy agency for Native Americans.
records.next_step: Open the database, enter your state or territory and choose the kind of organization you need. Then contact that organization directly.
constraints: It is a database, not a phone line.

records.name: The Arc: find your state or local chapter
records.org: The Arc of the United States
records.description: The Arc promotes and protects the human rights of people with intellectual and developmental disabilities. It is made up of 549 state and local chapters across the United States.
records.next_step: Use the chapter finder, choose your state and contact the chapter nearest you. Ask what help it offers with services, school, work and housing.

records.name: Autism Society National Helpline
records.description: Trained Information and Referral specialists talk with you about the resources and support options you are looking for and connect you to providers. The Helpline does not provide services itself.
records.next_step: Call 800-328-8476 and describe what you need, such as an evaluation, school support, adult services or support for a family.
constraints: The Autism Society says the Helpline is not a crisis line. In a crisis, call or text 988.
records.phone_note: 800-3-AUTISM

records.name: Easterseals: find a local service location
records.description: Easterseals has hundreds of service locations across the United States. Its listed areas of support include adult day services, assistive technology, autism services, camp and recreation, caregiving, early childhood programs, employment and job training, in-home care, mental health services, therapy and rehabilitation, transportation and mobility, and services for veterans and military families.
records.next_step: Search by ZIP code or state, then call the location nearest you and ask which services it offers and how to enroll.
constraints: Services differ by location.

records.name: Social Security: apply for disability benefits (SSDI and SSI)
records.description: Social Security runs the two main federal disability benefits. Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) is for people who have a disability or blindness and enough work history. Supplemental Security Income (SSI) is a separate program with its own rules, explained on ssa.gov/ssi.
records.next_step: Start the application online, call 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778), or use the office locator at ssa.gov/locator to find your local office. Ask what records to gather before you apply.
constraints: Phone lines are staffed 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. local time, Monday to Friday. Automated services run 24 hours a day.
records.phone_note: TTY 1-800-325-0778. Staffed weekdays, 8 a.m. to 7 p.m. local time

records.name: Social Security said no? Ask for reconsideration within 60 days
records.description: If Social Security denies a disability claim or makes a decision you disagree with, you can appeal. Social Security says to submit a request for reconsideration within 60 days of receiving the decision. There are four levels of appeal: reconsideration, a hearing with an administrative law judge, review by the Appeals Council and federal district court.
records.next_step: Find the date on your decision letter and file before 60 days pass. You can start the request online, upload form SSA-561, or call 1-800-772-1213 and say you want to request reconsideration.
constraints: Your state Protection and Advocacy agency or a legal aid office may be able to help; both are listed in this directory.

records.name: Medicaid: find your state agency to apply or ask about services
records.description: Medicaid.gov says to contact your state Medicaid agency to apply for Medicaid or CHIP, check your eligibility or an application, replace a card or find a provider. Its page lists the agency, phone number and website for every state and territory. Choose a state in this directory to see yours.
records.next_step: Choose your state above to see its Medicaid agency, or open the Medicaid.gov list and select your state.
constraints: Eligibility rules, income limits and covered services are different in every state.

records.name: HealthCare.gov call center: help with health coverage applications
records.description: The federal health insurance Marketplace phone line for individuals and families. It is open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, except holidays.
records.next_step: Call and say you want help applying for health coverage or have a question about an application.

records.name: ABLE accounts: save money without losing SSI or Medicaid
records.description: An ABLE account is a savings or investment account for qualified people with disabilities. The ABLE National Resource Center says the disability must have begun before age 46, and that up to $100,000 in an ABLE account is not counted as a resource for SSI. Money in the account, up to the plan’s limit, does not affect Medicaid eligibility.
records.next_step: Use the Center’s tools to compare state ABLE plans. Check your home state’s plan first, since it may offer a tax benefit. Most plans accept people who live in other states.
constraints: You must receive SSI or SSDI, or have a doctor certify your functional limitations.
After the account owner dies, Medicaid may seek repayment from the account, depending on state law.

records.name: Getting paid to care for a family member: where to ask
records.description: USAGov explains that some government programs pay family or friends of people with disabilities to help with daily activities such as personal care, giving medicine, cooking and cleaning. If the person already gets Medicaid, the state may let a family member or friend become a paid caregiver, often through what states call a consumer-directed personal assistance program. Other routes it lists are long-term care insurance, state paid family leave and, for veterans, VA programs such as Veteran-Directed Care and Aid and Attendance.
records.next_step: If the person has Medicaid, call your state Medicaid agency (listed under Income, benefits and health coverage) and ask about consumer-directed personal assistance. Otherwise call USAGov and ask which program fits.
constraints: Each state has different requirements and rules.
records.phone_note: USAGov, 1-844-USAGOV1, for questions about any government program

records.name: ARCH National Respite Locator: find a break for family caregivers
records.org: ARCH National Respite Network and Resource Center
records.description: A free search tool that helps parents, family caregivers and professionals find respite services in their state and local area. Listings are mainly home care agencies, assisted living and state or community agencies.
records.next_step: ARCH says to contact your State Respite Coalition or Lifespan Respite Program first to learn about providers and ways to pay, then search the Locator.
constraints: You are responsible for checking a provider’s experience, background checks and qualifications.
records.phone_note: ARCH office

records.name: SNAP food benefits: apply through your state office
records.description: SNAP helps people with low income buy food. You apply through your state or local SNAP office, not through USDA. USDA says monthly medical expenses over $35 can be deducted for elderly or disabled people, and that a household where everyone receives SSI does not need to meet an income limit.
records.next_step: Use the state directory to find your SNAP office, or call the USDA SNAP hotline. Tell the office about your disability and your monthly medical costs.
constraints: Income and resource limits apply; your local SNAP office can tell you where you stand.
records.phone_note: USDA SNAP hotline, English and Spanish

records.name: Lifeline: a monthly discount on phone or internet service
records.description: Lifeline is a federal program that lowers the monthly cost of phone or internet service by up to $9.25, or up to $34.25 on qualifying Tribal lands. You can qualify if you or someone in your household gets SSI, Medicaid, SNAP, federal public housing assistance or a Veterans Pension, or if your household income is at or below 135% of the federal poverty guidelines.
records.next_step: Apply at LifelineSupport.org or by mail, then sign up with a participating phone or internet company. If you have a disability and need help with the application, call the Lifeline Support Center.
constraints: One benefit per household, not per person.
records.phone_note: Lifeline Support Center, 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. Eastern, 7 days a week

records.name: Rental help: find your local Public Housing Agency (vouchers and public housing)
records.org: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
records.description: The Housing Choice Voucher program, also called Section 8, helps low-income families, older adults, veterans and people with disabilities afford housing in the private market. You apply through your local Public Housing Agency; about 2,000 of them run the program. HUD says waiting lists are long, so you may need to apply to more than one agency.
records.next_step: Find your local housing agency on the HUD site or call 1-800-955-2232. Ask whether the waiting list is open, whether there is a preference for people with disabilities and what documents to bring.
constraints: Your place on a waiting list depends on how many vouchers there are, when you applied and any preferences, such as disability or veteran status.
You do not have to live in an agency’s area to apply there.
HUD’s state pages also list a line for HUD-approved housing counselors, 1-800-569-4287, for advice on your own situation.
records.phone_note: HUD Customer Service Center, Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern

records.name: Job Accommodation Network (JAN): free advice on workplace accommodations
records.description: JAN gives free, confidential guidance on job accommodations and the Americans with Disabilities Act. Workers, job seekers, family members, employers and professionals can all use it.
records.next_step: Call or email JAN, describe your job and what is getting in the way, and ask which accommodations to request and how to put the request in writing.
constraints: Open 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern, Monday to Friday.

records.name: EEOC: file a job discrimination charge
records.description: The EEOC takes charges of job discrimination. It says you generally must file within 180 calendar days of the day the discrimination took place. The deadline is 300 days if a state or local agency enforces a law against the same discrimination.
records.next_step: Call, or use the EEOC Public Portal, to start. Write down dates, names and what was said, and count your deadline from the day it happened.
constraints: Federal employees and job applicants follow a different process and generally must contact their agency’s EEO counselor within 45 days.

records.name: Parent Centers: help for families of children and youth with disabilities
records.org: Center for Parent Information and Resources
records.description: Nearly 100 Parent Training and Information Centers and Community Parent Resource Centers serve families of children with disabilities, from birth to age 26, across the United States and its territories. They help parents take part in their child’s education and development.
records.next_step: Open the finder, choose your state and contact the center listed. Ask for help understanding your child’s school plan, your rights and what to do when you disagree with the school.
records.phone_note: National office of the Center for Parent Information and Resources, not a state center

records.name: 711 relay: phone calls for people who are deaf, hard of hearing or have a speech disability
records.description: Dial 711 from any telephone anywhere in the United States to reach a Telecommunications Relay Service communications assistant, who relays the call between you and the person you are calling. The FCC describes it as fast, functional and free. Voice callers can dial 711 to call someone who uses a TTY.
records.next_step: Dial 711, then give the number you want to call. You can use it to call any phone number listed in this directory.
constraints: 711 does not work for Video Relay Service, IP Relay or IP captioned telephone service; those start online or through your provider.
In an emergency, TTY users should call 911 directly instead of going through 711.

records.name: FCC Disability Rights Office and ASL Consumer Support Line
records.description: The Federal Communications Commission’s Disability Rights Office lists a voice line and an ASL Consumer Support Line that people who use American Sign Language can call by videophone.
records.next_step: Call by videophone in ASL, or by voice, and describe the problem you are having with a phone, relay, captioning or other communication service.
records.phone_note: Voice. ASL videophone: 1-844-432-2275

records.name: Hearing Loss Association of America: chapters and hearing aid cost information
records.description: A national organization for people with hearing loss. Its site lists local chapters, a financial assistance page, information on hearing aids, cochlear implants and assistive listening systems, and pages for parents and veterans.
records.next_step: Call or email and ask for the chapter nearest you. Open the Financial Assistance page if the cost of hearing aids is the problem.

records.name: National Association of the Deaf: contact and video calls
records.description: The National Association of the Deaf takes general questions through a front desk line and a contact form, and says it will set up a video call with you if you email.
records.next_step: Use the contact form or call the front desk line, and say what you need help with.
records.phone_note: Front desk line for general inquiries

records.name: APH ConnectCenter: information and a directory of services for people who are blind or have low vision
records.org: American Printing House for the Blind
records.description: Free resources and support for blind and visually impaired people and their families, from the American Printing House for the Blind. It includes FamilyConnect for families, CareerConnect for school, work and transition, VisionAware, and a Directory of Resources for finding educational, rehabilitation and community-based services.
records.next_step: Open the Directory of Resources and search for services near you.

records.name: National Library Service (NLS): braille and audio books for people who cannot read regular print
records.description: The Library of Congress service for people who struggle to read print because of a visual, physical, reading or other disability, including low vision or blindness, dyslexia and physical disabilities that make it hard to use a book. Books come in braille and audio, by mail or by download.
records.next_step: Call 1-888-657-7323 to find your network library, or apply online. A professional such as a doctor, nurse, teacher, librarian or social worker must confirm that you qualify; your network librarian can often do this by phone.
constraints: For U.S. residents and U.S. citizens living abroad.
records.phone_note: 1-888-NLS-READ

records.name: Hadley: learning and support for people with vision loss, at no cost
records.description: Hadley offers practical solutions, emotional support and community connection for people with vision loss, including live discussions and peer support. Hadley says there is no cost, no waitlist and no barriers.
records.next_step: Call, or create an account on the website or in the Hadley Helps app.
records.phone_note: Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Central

records.name: American Council of the Blind
records.description: A national organization whose site lists accessibility services, community events, scholarships, an audio description project and advocacy. It also offers help in Spanish by email at bienvenidos@acb.org.
records.next_step: Call or email and say what you are looking for.

records.name: Helen Keller National Center: training for people who are DeafBlind
records.description: A national program that provides vocational rehabilitation services to people with combined hearing and vision loss: youth 16 and older, working-age adults and adults 55 and older, in the United States and its territories. Services include training in adaptive technology, communication, independent living, orientation and mobility, and work skills. It has a network of regional representatives.
records.next_step: Open the website, find the regional representative for your area and ask how to apply.

records.name: Parkinson’s Foundation Helpline
records.description: Helpline specialists answer questions about Parkinson’s disease, including diagnosis, treatment, daily living and caregiving. They refer callers to health professionals, support groups, wellness classes and organizations that may help with medication, transportation, basic needs or respite care. Help is offered in English and Spanish.
records.next_step: Call or email with your questions and ask for support groups and specialists near you.
constraints: Open Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. Eastern.
The Foundation does not give financial aid directly.
records.phone_note: 1-800-4PD-INFO

records.name: Epilepsy Foundation Helpline
records.description: The Helpline gives support by phone, email and online form on epilepsy treatments, medication questions, support groups, seizure first aid, safety devices, and employment and discrimination concerns, and refers callers to local Epilepsy Foundation offices.
records.next_step: Call and say what you need. Ask for the local office or support group nearest you.
constraints: Open Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Eastern, except holidays.

records.name: Alzheimer’s Association 24/7 Helpline
records.description: A free helpline open around the clock, 365 days a year, for people living with memory loss, Alzheimer’s or dementia and for caregivers. Staff give information, help with care planning and finding care providers, guidance on housing and respite care, and emotional support. Help is available in more than 200 languages through interpreters.
records.next_step: Call any time. If you use a TTY or relay, dial 711 first.

records.name: Civil legal aid for people with low income: find an office near you
records.description: The Legal Services Corporation funds 129 independent nonprofit legal aid programs, with more than 800 offices in every state, the District of Columbia and the U.S. territories. They help people with low income with civil legal problems involving safety, basic income and family stability, including evictions and other housing matters. LSC says its programs serve households with income at or below 125% of the federal poverty guidelines.
records.next_step: Enter your address or city in the Get Legal Help search to find the office that serves you, then call or apply online. LawHelp.org has legal information and free forms.
constraints: Each office decides which cases it can take.
For a criminal case, ask the court for a court-appointed lawyer.

records.name: Health care or social services discrimination: file a complaint with the HHS Office for Civil Rights
records.org: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Civil Rights
records.description: You can file a complaint with the HHS Office for Civil Rights if you believe you were discriminated against because of a disability in a program that HHS runs or funds, or by a state or local government health care or social services agency. You can file for yourself or for someone else.
records.next_step: File through the OCR Complaint Portal. Write down what happened, when and where, and file as soon as you can.
constraints: This office does not generally investigate housing, employment or education complaints; other offices in this directory handle those.

records.name: School or college discrimination: file a complaint with the Office for Civil Rights
records.org: U.S. Department of Education, Office for Civil Rights
records.description: The Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights can investigate discrimination complaints based on disability, among other grounds. You can file with an electronic complaint form or a fillable PDF form.
records.next_step: Open the page and use the electronic complaint form. Write down what happened, when and who was involved. The page does not state the deadline, so file soon and ask the office or a Parent Center how long you have.

records.name: Voting with a disability: your rights and who to call
records.org: vote.gov and the U.S. Election Assistance Commission
records.description: Federal law protects your right to vote privately and independently. Vote.gov says you have a right to accessibility accommodations whether you vote in person or by mail, such as a wheelchair-accessible voting location, at least one accessible voting device at every location, materials in large print and someone to help you vote, as long as that person is not your employer or union representative.
records.next_step: Contact your state or local election office before Election Day and say exactly what you need. If your voting location is not accessible, ask about curbside voting, another location or voting by mail. If you are turned away, call your state Protection and Advocacy agency.
constraints: Rules for mail ballots, curbside voting and voter ID are set by each state.
You can report disability discrimination in voting to the Department of Justice.
records.phone_note: U.S. Election Assistance Commission

records.name: Amtrak: accessible travel, reservations and the disability discount
records.description: Amtrak takes reservations for accessible seating, space for a wheeled mobility device and accessible rooms online, by phone, by TTY or at a ticket counter. Adults with a disability get a 10% discount on the rail fare, and so does one companion.
records.next_step: Book online or call 1-800-872-7245 and say what you need. When you can, ask for any change to Amtrak’s usual practices at least 72 hours before departure.
constraints: Some routes ask for proof of disability to get the discount.
Train crews do not provide personal care; travel with an attendant if you need that help.
records.phone_note: 1-800-USA-RAIL. TTY 1-800-523-6590, or dial 711. Text the same number 7 a.m. to 11 p.m. Eastern

records.name: Alabama Medicaid: apply for Medicaid and ask about in-home services
records.description: This is the contact Medicaid.gov lists for Alabama to apply for Medicaid or CHIP, check your eligibility or an application, replace a card or find a provider. Many of the waiver, equipment and in-home help programs in this directory are paid for through Medicaid.
records.next_step: Call or open the website and say you want to apply for Medicaid, or check on an application. If you already have Medicaid, ask how to request in-home help or a waiver, whether there is a waiting list and how to appeal if you are turned down.
constraints: Eligibility rules, income limits and covered services are different in every state.
If the person already gets Medicaid, the state may let a family member or friend be paid as a caregiver; ask about consumer-directed personal assistance.
records.phone_note: As listed by Medicaid.gov.

records.name: Alaska Medicaid: apply for Medicaid and ask about in-home services
records.description: This is the contact Medicaid.gov lists for Alaska to apply for Medicaid or CHIP, check your eligibility or an application, replace a card or find a provider. Many of the waiver, equipment and in-home help programs in this directory are paid for through Medicaid.
records.next_step: Call or open the website and say you want to apply for Medicaid, or check on an application. If you already have Medicaid, ask how to request in-home help or a waiver, whether there is a waiting list and how to appeal if you are turned down.
constraints: Eligibility rules, income limits and covered services are different in every state.
If the person already gets Medicaid, the state may let a family member or friend be paid as a caregiver; ask about consumer-directed personal assistance.
records.phone_note: As listed by Medicaid.gov. Eligibility line. Coverage and billing questions: 800-780-9972.

records.name: American Samoa Medicaid Office: apply for Medicaid
records.description: This is the contact Medicaid.gov lists for American Samoa to apply for Medicaid or CHIP, check your eligibility or an application, replace a card or find a provider.
records.next_step: Call or open the website and say you want to apply for Medicaid, or check on an application. Ask what services are covered and how to appeal if you are turned down.
constraints: Eligibility rules and covered services are set locally; ask what is covered.
records.phone_note: As listed by Medicaid.gov.

records.name: Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System (AHCCCS): apply for Medicaid and ask about in-home services
records.org: Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System (AHCCCS)
records.description: This is the contact Medicaid.gov lists for Arizona to apply for Medicaid or CHIP, check your eligibility or an application, replace a card or find a provider. Many of the waiver, equipment and in-home help programs in this directory are paid for through Medicaid.
records.next_step: Call or open the website and say you want to apply for Medicaid, or check on an application. If you already have Medicaid, ask how to request in-home help or a waiver, whether there is a waiting list and how to appeal if you are turned down.
constraints: Eligibility rules, income limits and covered services are different in every state.
If the person already gets Medicaid, the state may let a family member or friend be paid as a caregiver; ask about consumer-directed personal assistance.
records.phone_note: As listed by Medicaid.gov. Outside Maricopa County. In Maricopa County: 602-417-4000. From out of state: 800-523-0231.

records.name: Arkansas Medicaid: apply for Medicaid and ask about in-home services
records.description: This is the contact Medicaid.gov lists for Arkansas to apply for Medicaid or CHIP, check your eligibility or an application, replace a card or find a provider. Many of the waiver, equipment and in-home help programs in this directory are paid for through Medicaid.
records.next_step: Call or open the website and say you want to apply for Medicaid, or check on an application. If you already have Medicaid, ask how to request in-home help or a waiver, whether there is a waiting list and how to appeal if you are turned down.
constraints: Eligibility rules, income limits and covered services are different in every state.
If the person already gets Medicaid, the state may let a family member or friend be paid as a caregiver; ask about consumer-directed personal assistance.
records.phone_note: As listed by Medicaid.gov. Other numbers listed: 800-482-8988 and 501-682-8233.

records.name: California Department of Health Care Services (Medi-Cal): apply for Medicaid and ask about in-home services
records.org: California Department of Health Care Services (Medi-Cal)
records.description: This is the contact Medicaid.gov lists for California to apply for Medicaid or CHIP, check your eligibility or an application, replace a card or find a provider. Many of the waiver, equipment and in-home help programs in this directory are paid for through Medicaid.
records.next_step: Call or open the website and say you want to apply for Medicaid, or check on an application. If you already have Medicaid, ask how to request in-home help or a waiver, whether there is a waiting list and how to appeal if you are turned down.
constraints: Eligibility rules, income limits and covered services are different in every state.
If the person already gets Medicaid, the state may let a family member or friend be paid as a caregiver; ask about consumer-directed personal assistance.
records.phone_note: As listed by Medicaid.gov. Also listed: 916-636-1980.

records.name: Health First Colorado: apply for Medicaid and ask about in-home services
records.description: This is the contact Medicaid.gov lists for Colorado to apply for Medicaid or CHIP, check your eligibility or an application, replace a card or find a provider. Many of the waiver, equipment and in-home help programs in this directory are paid for through Medicaid.
records.next_step: Call or open the website and say you want to apply for Medicaid, or check on an application. If you already have Medicaid, ask how to request in-home help or a waiver, whether there is a waiting list and how to appeal if you are turned down.
constraints: Eligibility rules, income limits and covered services are different in every state.
If the person already gets Medicaid, the state may let a family member or friend be paid as a caregiver; ask about consumer-directed personal assistance.

records.next_step: Call or open the website and say you want to apply for Medicaid, or check on an application. If you already have Medicaid, ask how to request in-home help or a waiver, whether there is a waiting list and how to appeal if you are turned down.
constraints: Eligibility rules, income limits and covered services are different in every state.
If the person already gets Medicaid, the state may let a family member or friend be paid as a caregiver; ask about consumer-directed personal assistance.
records.phone_note: As listed by Medicaid.gov.

records.name: LIHEAP: help paying heating and cooling bills
records.org: Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (state and territory offices)
records.description: The Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program helps with heating or cooling bills and with emergency services during an energy crisis. USA.gov says electric bills may be covered depending on where you live. Eligibility is based on income, and each state or territory sets its own rules.
records.next_step: Use the search tool to find your state or territory LIHEAP office, or call the NEAR hotline for a referral, then ask how to apply. Some offices take applications online; others require a visit in person.
constraints: Income limits and what is covered are set by each state or territory.
If getting to an office is hard for you, ask how else you can apply.
LIHEAP never charges a fee to apply. If someone asks you for a fee, report it to the HHS fraud hotline at 1-800-447-8477.
records.phone_note: National Energy Assistance Referral (NEAR) hotline, weekdays 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. Eastern, as listed on the federal LIHEAP program page
records.contact_how: Find your state or territory office with the LIHEAP search tool.

records.name: Utility shut-off notice: check your state’s disconnection rules
records.org: LIHEAP Clearinghouse (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services)
records.description: Rules on when a utility may disconnect service are set state by state. USA.gov says state policies vary based on weather, age, disability and the utility provider. The LIHEAP Clearinghouse lists each state’s policy and contacts.
records.next_step: Find your state on the list and read its rule. Then call your utility before the shut-off date, tell them about a disability or medical equipment in the home, and ask which protections and payment arrangements apply to you.
constraints: Protections are different in every state and may depend on the season and the kind of utility.
records.contact_how: Look up your state’s rule on the list, then call the utility named on your bill.

records.name: Weatherization Assistance Program: home improvements that lower energy bills
records.org: U.S. Department of Energy (state weatherization offices)
records.description: The Weatherization Assistance Program makes home improvements that save energy and money. USA.gov says you may qualify based on income, or because you receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI) or Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF).
records.next_step: Open the Department of Energy page to find your state weatherization office and ask how to apply.
constraints: Each state runs its own program and sets its own steps.
records.contact_how: Find your state weatherization office on the Department of Energy page.

records.name: National Hunger Hotline: find food near you
records.description: USA.gov lists this USDA hotline among the ways to get emergency food. It answers in English and Spanish, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Eastern time. USA.gov’s advice if you are hungry now: call 211 to find food in your area.
records.next_step: Call 1-866-348-6479 (1-866-3-HUNGRY). For Spanish, call 1-877-842-6273 (1-877-8-HAMBRE). Outside those hours call 211, or enter your ZIP code in HUD’s Find Shelter tool to look up a food pantry.
constraints: Open Monday through Friday. It is not a 24-hour line.
records.phone_note: Spanish: 1-877-842-6273. Monday to Friday, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. Eastern

records.name: Home-delivered meals: ask your Area Agency on Aging
records.description: Area Agencies on Aging offer home-delivered meals, brought to older adults and people with disabilities who have difficulty leaving home. The local agency decides who is eligible, based on being 60 or older and on needs such as limited mobility or no way to prepare meals. A spouse of any age, a caregiver or a person with a disability who lives with an eligible older adult may also be able to get meals.
records.next_step: Call, text or use a videophone to reach the Eldercare Locator at 1-800-677-1116 and ask for the Area Agency on Aging that serves your address. Ask that agency about home-delivered meals and whether there is a waiting list. If there is, ask what other meal delivery is available locally.
constraints: The federal program is for people 60 and older, with limited exceptions for people with disabilities who live with them. If you are younger, call 211 and ask what meal delivery your area offers.
There is no income test. You may be asked for a voluntary contribution toward the meal.
records.phone_note: Eldercare Locator: voice, videophone or text

records.name: Food programs for adults 60 and older with limited income
records.org: USDA Food and Nutrition Service (state agencies)
records.description: Two USDA programs for adults 60 or older with limited income. The Commodity Supplemental Food Program gives a monthly package of food, picked up at a local agency; some states deliver. The Senior Farmers Market Nutrition Program gives coupons for fresh produce and is not offered in every state.
records.next_step: Find your state contact on the USDA list and ask how to apply and whether delivery is available where you live.
constraints: For people 60 or older who meet the income limit.
Not every program operates in every state.
records.contact_how: Find your state contact on the USDA Food and Nutrition Service list.

records.name: Nowhere to stay tonight: find emergency shelter
records.org: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development and 211
records.description: HUD’s direction for people who are homeless: dial 211 and press 6 for homeless services. HUD’s Find Shelter tool lists local shelters, food pantries, health clinics and places to get clothing. USA.gov says 211 works in most areas of the United States and gives referrals for emergency housing.
records.next_step: Call 211 first. Say you have a disability and what you need in a shelter, such as a ground-floor bed, room for a wheelchair, a service animal or a place to keep medication cold. If 211 does not work where you are, use the Find Shelter tool.
constraints: Shelter space changes daily. Call before you travel.
In immediate danger, call 911.
records.phone_note: HUD says to press 6 for homeless services

records.name: HUD-approved housing counselors: advice on your housing situation
records.org: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
records.description: HUD keeps a list of approved housing counseling agencies and describes them as a place to get advice on your specific housing needs. HUD lists them for both renters and homeowners.
records.next_step: Search for a counseling agency near you, or call (800) 569-4287. Tell the counselor about your disability-related needs, such as an accessible unit or a voucher, and ask what they can help you apply for.
constraints: Ask whether there is any fee before you start.
records.phone_note: HUD housing counseling line

records.description: A type of housing voucher that helps people under 62 who have a disability find and pay for private rental housing. USA.gov says the person with the disability must be the head of the household, the spouse or a co-head, and the household must meet income and location requirements.
records.next_step: Contact your local Public Housing Agency and ask whether it has Non-Elderly Disabled vouchers and how to get on the list. To find your agency, use the HUD list or call 1-800-955-2232.
constraints: Ask whether the agency has these vouchers and whether its waiting list is open.
records.phone_note: HUD Public and Indian Housing Information Resource Center

records.phone_note: 24 hours a day. Also written 1-877-4AID-VET

records.description: USA.gov lists this line under emergency housing for teens and youth. It offers free, confidential support 24 hours a day, and can arrange free transportation home or to other safe, stable housing.

records.phone_note: 24 hours a day. Also written 1-800-RUNAWAY

records.name: American Job Centers: free job search and training help near you
records.description: Nearly 2,300 American Job Centers give free help to job seekers: job search assistance, career counseling, job training services, practice interviews, and resource rooms with phones, internet and resume tools. CareerOneStop lists accessibility and special accommodations for people with disabilities among their services.
records.next_step: Use the finder to locate a center, or call 1-877-872-5627 (1-877-US2-JOBS). Tell the center which accommodations you need before your visit.
constraints: Some centers offer the full range of services and others refer you elsewhere for part of it. Ask what your nearest center does on site.
records.phone_note: Also written 1-877-US2-JOBS. TTY: 1-877-889-5627

records.name: Federal jobs: the hiring path for people with disabilities
