records.description: USA.gov points job seekers with disabilities to the USAJOBS hiring path for individuals with disabilities, and to the Office of Personnel Management’s list of Selective Placement Program Coordinators at federal agencies.
records.next_step: Read the USAJOBS page on the hiring path for individuals with disabilities. Then look up the Selective Placement Program Coordinator at the agency where you want to work and ask how to apply.
records.contact_how: Start on the USAJOBS page; each federal agency has its own coordinator.

records.name: AbilityOne: jobs with nonprofit agencies for people who are blind or have significant disabilities
records.description: USA.gov describes AbilityOne as a program that helps people who are blind or have significant disabilities find jobs with nonprofit agencies nationwide.
records.next_step: Start at AbilityOne.gov. If you have a vocational rehabilitation counselor, ask whether an AbilityOne job fits your work goal.
records.contact_how: Start on the AbilityOne website.

records.name: Veteran Readiness and Employment (VR&E)
records.description: Support for veterans with disabilities related to their service: training, counseling, help finding and keeping a job, and help starting a business.
records.next_step: Open the VA page to see the program tracks and how to apply. A county veterans service office can help you file; see Veteran benefits in this directory.
records.contact_how: Apply through VA; the VA page linked here has the steps.

records.name: Adapting a vehicle: evaluation, equipment, dealers and who may pay
records.description: NHTSA’s guidance for drivers and passengers with disabilities. It says to consult a driver rehabilitation specialist before you buy, so you learn what equipment you need, avoid paying for equipment you do not need and hear about financial help. NHTSA says a new vehicle modified with adaptive equipment can cost $20,000 to $80,000, that programs may help pay part or all of a modification, and that most major manufacturers offer rebates on adaptive equipment.
records.next_step: Before buying anything, ask your state vocational rehabilitation agency whether it can help pay for a driving evaluation or a modification. Veterans can ask VA. Use NHTSA’s search to check that a mobility equipment dealer is registered with NHTSA as a vehicle modifier.
constraints: NHTSA says vocational rehabilitation and workers’ compensation agencies may help with the cost of a driver evaluation, and that auto insurance may cover all or part of adaptive equipment.
Take the equipment you normally use, such as a walker, to a driving evaluation.
records.phone_note: NHTSA Vehicle Safety Hotline. TTY: 888-275-9171

records.name: Find a driver rehabilitation specialist (ADED directory)
records.org: ADED: The Association for Driver Rehabilitation Specialists
records.description: Driver rehabilitation specialists evaluate a person’s abilities, provide driver training, help with the state licensing process and work with mobility equipment dealers on vehicle fit. ADED trains and certifies them and keeps a searchable directory of providers and mobility equipment dealers. NHTSA names ADED as the place to find a qualified specialist.
records.next_step: Open the provider search. For the widest results, enter only your state in the location field. ADED says a referral can come from a doctor, an occupational therapist, a family member or you.
constraints: An evaluation generally has two parts: a clinical assessment and a behind-the-wheel assessment.
A listing in the directory is not an endorsement. Ask about experience with your kind of equipment and what the evaluation costs.
records.contact_how: Search the ADED directory by state, then contact the provider directly.

records.name: Disabled parking placards and plates: apply through your state
records.org: State motor vehicle agencies (federal guideline: 23 CFR Part 1235)
records.description: Each state issues its own parking placards and license plates for people with disabilities that limit or impair the ability to walk. The federal guideline to states calls for a physician’s certification with the first application, a temporary placard good for up to six months when the disability is temporary, and recognition of placards and plates issued by other states.
records.next_step: Start at your state motor vehicle agency’s website and search for “disability placard.” It should have the form or name the office that handles it. Ask your doctor’s office to complete the medical certification. USA.gov links to every state and territory agency.
constraints: The federal rule is a guideline. Each state sets its own form, fee, renewal period and who may certify.
When you travel, the guideline calls for other states to recognize your placard or plate.
records.contact_how: Apply through your state motor vehicle agency; USA.gov lists each one.

records.name: Early intervention for babies and toddlers: how to ask for a free evaluation
records.org: Center for Parent Information and Resources
records.description: Early intervention is a system of services for babies and toddlers who have a developmental delay or disability. It is required by Part C of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) and is available in every state and territory. Parents do not have to wait for a referral, and the evaluation is free.
records.next_step: Find your state on the ECTA Center list and call the referral number shown. Say you are concerned about your child’s development and want an evaluation under Part C of IDEA. Write down the name of each person you speak with and the date.
constraints: For children under age three. If your child is three or older, ask your school district for a special education evaluation, which is also free.
The evaluation and service coordination are free. Depending on state policy, some services may have a sliding-scale fee. A child cannot be denied services because the family cannot pay.
For an eligible child, the steps from referral to a written service plan (an Individualized Family Service Plan) should take 45 days.
The overview is also available in Spanish at parentcenterhub.org/parabebes.
records.contact_how: Use the state list to find your program’s referral number.

records.name: Early intervention for babies and toddlers (birth to age 3)
records.org: Alabama Early Intervention System; Department of Rehabilitation Services
records.description: The early intervention program in Alabama serves children from birth to age three who have a developmental delay or disability. Parents do not have to wait for a referral, and the evaluation is free.
records.next_step: Call the referral line. Say you are concerned about your child’s development and want an evaluation under Part C of IDEA. Write down the name of each person you speak with and the date.
constraints: For children under age three. If your child is three or older, ask your school district for a special education evaluation, which is also free.
The evaluation and service coordination are free. Depending on state policy, some services may have a sliding-scale fee. A child cannot be denied services because the family cannot pay.
For an eligible child, the steps from referral to a written service plan (an Individualized Family Service Plan) should take 45 days.

records.name: Early intervention for babies and toddlers (birth to age 3)
records.description: The early intervention program in the U.S. Virgin Islands serves children from birth to age three who have a developmental delay or disability. Parents do not have to wait for a referral, and the evaluation is free.
records.next_step: Call the program office, or use its website, and ask how to refer your child where you live. Say you are concerned about your child’s development and want an evaluation under Part C of IDEA. Write down the name of each person you speak with and the date.
constraints: For children under age three. If your child is three or older, ask your school district for a special education evaluation, which is also free.

records.name: Family-to-Family Health Information Centers: free help for families of children with special health care needs
records.org: Family Voices and the federal Maternal and Child Health Bureau
records.description: Family-led centers that support families of children and youth with special health care needs. The federal Maternal and Child Health Bureau funds one in every state, the District of Columbia and five territories, and three that serve tribal communities. Staff are family members with first-hand experience. Help is free to families.
records.next_step: Choose your state or territory in the Family Voices finder and call the center listed. Say what your child needs and where you are stuck.
constraints: The centers help with health coverage, finding services and connecting with other families. They are not medical providers.
records.contact_how: Find your state’s center with the Family Voices finder.

records.name: VA automobile allowance and adaptive equipment
records.description: VA can help an eligible veteran or service member buy a specially equipped vehicle and can pay for adaptive equipment. You may be eligible if you have a service-connected disability that includes loss or permanent loss of use of a hand or foot, permanently reduced vision in both eyes, a severe burn injury or ALS. Ankylosis of a knee or hip qualifies for the adaptive-equipment grant only.
records.next_step: Apply online or by mail with VA Form 21-4502 before you buy anything, and wait for VA’s approval. VA pays the vehicle allowance to the seller and must approve adaptive equipment before it is bought. A county veterans service office can help you file.
constraints: Do not buy the vehicle or the equipment until VA has authorized it.
Adaptive equipment may be provided for no more than two vehicles in a four-year period.
There is no time limit for filing the claim.
records.phone_note: VA benefits line, as printed on the application form. TTY: 711

records.name: Services for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing
records.org: State agency for people who are deaf or hard of hearing
records.description: Arkansas Rehabilitation Services’ Deaf and Hard of Hearing program has staff interpreters, trains and advises agencies and businesses such as hospitals, 911 centers and police on removing communication barriers, and runs a Telecommunications Access Program for communication devices.
records.next_step: Contact the agency using the phone, videophone or email shown here, and say what you need, such as an interpreter or captioner, phone equipment, advocacy or help for your family. Ask who to contact if the agency does not offer it.
constraints: What these agencies do differs from state to state. Some provide services directly; others advise the state.
records.phone_note: Arkansas Rehabilitation Services, as listed on the program’s page

records.org: State agency for people who are deaf or hard of hearing
records.description: The Arizona Commission for the Deaf and the Hard of Hearing shares resources, helps people advocate for their communication needs, trains service providers, and runs AzTEDP, which gives amplified phones, TTYs, speech devices and flashing or vibrating alerts at no cost to U.S. citizens living in Arizona who are deaf, hard of hearing, deafblind or speech-impaired, regardless of income.

constraints: For the equipment program, call AzTEDP at 602-542-3365 or videophone 602-761-9541, as listed on the commission’s site.
What these agencies do differs from state to state. Some provide services directly; others advise the state.

records.name: Office of Deaf Access
records.org: State agency for people who are deaf or hard of hearing
records.description: California’s Office of Deaf Access runs the Deaf Access Program, created in 1980 so that deaf and hard of hearing children, adults and families can use public programs. Through regional agencies, the program provides qualified sign language interpreters, including emergency sign language services 24 hours a day, 7 days a week for medical, legal or civil emergencies.

constraints: Services are delivered by regional agencies around the state; the office can tell you which one serves your county.

Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.contact_how: Apply through the agency’s page, which lists its offices and how to reach them.

records.name: Disability parking placard in New Hampshire: how to apply
records.org: New Hampshire Division of Motor Vehicles (DMV)
records.description: In New Hampshire, disability parking placards are issued by the New Hampshire Division of Motor Vehicles (DMV). Apply with the Application for Walking Disability Privileges (RDMV130). Who can certify the disability: a licensed physician, physician associate, podiatrist or advanced practice registered nurse, who describes the condition and how it limits walking.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Apply at any DMV registration office, leave it in a DMV drop box with a copy of your license or ID, or mail it to NH Dept. of Safety, DMV - Registration, 23 Hazen Drive, Concord, NH 03305.
constraints: A temporary placard is authorized for up to six months.
A permanent placard lasts up to five years and expires with your driver license or non-driver ID. Walking disability plates with one placard cost $8.
Vehicles with a walking disability plate or placard may park free at city and town meters and public lots that charge a fee, within local time limits.
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.contact_how: Apply through the agency’s page, which lists its offices and how to reach them.

records.name: Disability parking placard in New Jersey: how to apply
records.description: In New Jersey, disability parking placards are issued by the New Jersey Motor Vehicle Commission (MVC). Apply with the Application for Vehicle License Plates and/or Placard for Persons with a Disability (SP-41). Who can certify the disability: a medical practitioner, who also attaches a prescription or letterhead statement; a U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs representative for veterans rated 100% permanently disabled.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Bring the form to a motor vehicle agency for same-day processing, or mail it to NJ Motor Vehicle Commission, Special Plate Unit, PO Box 015, Trenton, NJ 08666-0015. The medical certification must be dated within 60 days.
constraints: Temporary placards are issued by your municipal chief of police, not the MVC: apply in person (form SP-68). They last six months, with one six-month renewal.
There is no fee for plates or a placard. Permanent placards and plates need a new medical certification every three years.
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.phone_note: MVC Special Plate Unit, as printed on form SP-41

records.name: Disability parking placard in New Mexico: how to apply
records.description: In New Mexico, disability parking placards are issued by the New Mexico Motor Vehicle Division (MVD). Apply with the Certificate of Eligibility for Parking Placard for Mobility Impaired Individuals (MVD-10383). Who can certify the disability: a health care practitioner, who completes the medical statement on the form.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Take the completed form to an MVD office or MVD service provider.
constraints: A temporary placard can be issued for up to one year.
A permanent placard lasts four years and does not need new medical information to renew. There is no fee for disability plates. MVD does not mail a reminder before a placard expires.
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.contact_how: Apply through the agency’s page, which lists its offices and how to reach them.

records.name: Disability parking placard in New York: how to apply
records.org: Local city, town or village issuing agents (New York State DMV issues plates only)
records.description: In New York, disability parking permits are issued by local city, town or village offices, usually the clerk. The state DMV issues disability plates only. Apply with the Application for a Parking Permit or License Plates for Persons with Severe Disabilities (MV-664.1). Who can certify the disability: a physician, physician assistant, nurse practitioner, podiatrist (for foot-related disabilities) or optometrist (for blindness), on the form or on letterhead.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Take it to the office that issues permits where you live, usually your city, town or village clerk. Do not send it to DMV, which does not issue parking permits. New York City residents mail it to the NYC Department of Transportation.
constraints: There is no fee for a permit.

New York City residents can also get a separate city permit for curbside parking from NYC DOT (718-433-3100). Outside New York City, the same local office issues metered parking waivers (form MV-664.1MP).
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.contact_how: Apply through the agency’s page, which lists its offices and how to reach them.

records.name: Disability parking placard in North Carolina: how to apply
records.org: North Carolina Division of Motor Vehicles (NCDMV)
records.description: In North Carolina, disability parking placards are issued by the North Carolina Division of Motor Vehicles (NCDMV). Apply with the Application for Disability Parking Placard (MVR-37A). Who can certify the disability: a physician, physician assistant or nurse practitioner, an authorized representative of the Division of Services for the Blind, or U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs documentation.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Get it the same day at a license plate agency, or mail it to NCDMV, 3148 Mail Service Center, Raleigh, NC 27697-3148 and allow three to four weeks.
constraints: A temporary placard is valid for up to six months and cannot be renewed.

Placards cost $5 each (limit two). A regular placard is valid for five years and needs a new medical certification to renew unless you are 80 or older or certified as totally and permanently disabled.
North Carolina drivers who are deaf or hard of hearing can also ask for a voluntary hearing-loss symbol on their driver license.
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.contact_how: Apply through the agency’s page, which lists its offices and how to reach them.

records.name: Disability parking placard in North Dakota: how to apply
records.org: North Dakota Department of Transportation, Motor Vehicle Division
records.description: In North Dakota, disability parking placards are issued by the North Dakota Department of Transportation, Motor Vehicle Division. Apply with the Application for Mobility-Impaired Parking Permit (SFN 2886). Who can certify the disability: a physician, chiropractor, physician assistant, advanced practice registered nurse or physical therapist.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Apply at a motor vehicle office (driver’s license offices do not issue permits) or by mail to the ND Department of Transportation, Motor Vehicle Division, Bismarck, ND 58505-0780. Offices outside Bismarck may add a service fee.
constraints: A temporary (red) permit is issued three months at a time and costs $3.
There is no fee for a permanent permit. A permit for a non-reversible condition renews without a new medical signature.
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.contact_how: Apply through the agency’s page, which lists its offices and how to reach them.

records.name: Disability parking placard in Ohio: how to apply
records.description: In Ohio, disability parking placards are issued by the Ohio Bureau of Motor Vehicles (BMV). Apply with the Application for Removable Windshield Placards (BMV 4826). Who can certify the disability: a health care provider, who writes a prescription giving the date, your name, a statement that it is for a removable windshield placard, how long the condition is expected to last, and the provider’s signature.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Bring the application and prescription to a deputy registrar license agency.
constraints: Veterans and active-duty service members with a service-connected disability that limits walking can get a free placard with form BMV 4531.
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.contact_how: Apply through the agency’s page, which lists its offices and how to reach them.

records.name: Disability parking placard in Oklahoma: how to apply
records.description: In Oklahoma, disability parking placards are issued by Service Oklahoma. Apply with the Physical Disability Parking Placard Application (302DC). Who can certify the disability: a physician licensed in medicine or surgery, osteopathic medicine, chiropractic, podiatric medicine or optometry; a licensed physician assistant; or a licensed and certified advanced registered nurse practitioner.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Apply online, and your physician gets an email to finish their part. Or mail the paper form to Service Oklahoma, P.O. Box 11415, Oklahoma City, OK 73136, or drop it off at 6015 N Classen Blvd., Oklahoma City. Applications expire 60 days after the physician signs.
constraints: A temporary placard lasts no more than six months.
Placards are free. A regular placard lasts five years.
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.phone_note: Service Oklahoma Disability Parking Permit Desk, as listed on its placard page

records.name: Disability parking placard in Oregon: how to apply
records.description: In Oregon, disability parking placards are issued by the Oregon Driver & Motor Vehicle Services (DMV). Apply with the Application for Individual Disabled Person Parking Permit Placard (735-265). Who can certify the disability: a doctor of medicine or osteopathy, podiatrist, chiropractor, naturopath, nurse practitioner, physician associate or licensed optometrist.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Take it to any DMV office and leave with your placard, or send it by fax (503-945-5181), by email (ORDMVDriverTrans@odot.oregon.gov) or by mail to DMV Driver Transactions Unit, 1905 Lana Ave NE, Salem, OR 97314.
constraints: A temporary permit lasts up to six months.
Permits are free. Individual and wheelchair-user permits last eight years.

People whose disability makes a DMV visit impractical or harmful can get a parking ID card and permit by mail. Veterans with a 50% or greater service-connected disability can add an Oregon Wounded Warrior sticker.
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.phone_note: Oregon DMV Customer Assistance (TTY 711), as listed on the parking permit page

records.name: Disability parking placard in Pennsylvania: how to apply
records.description: In Pennsylvania, disability parking placards are issued by the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT). Apply with the Person with Disability Parking Placard Application (MV-145A). Who can certify the disability: a physician, chiropractor, optometrist, podiatrist, physician assistant or certified registered nurse practitioner licensed in Pennsylvania or a neighboring state; a police officer can certify blindness or loss of full use of a leg for a permanent placard.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Mail it to PennDOT Bureau of Motor Vehicles, P.O. Box 68268, Harrisburg, PA 17106-8268. Some approved health care facilities can hand out temporary placards on the spot.
constraints: A temporary placard lasts up to six months and cannot be extended.
There is no fee. A permanent placard lasts five years and can be renewed online.
On request, local authorities may post a reserved parking sign on the street near the home of a person with a disability placard or plate.
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.contact_how: Apply through the agency’s page, which lists its offices and how to reach them.

records.name: Disability parking placard in Rhode Island: how to apply
records.org: Rhode Island Division of Motor Vehicles, Disability Parking Placards Office
records.description: In Rhode Island, disability parking placards are issued by the Rhode Island Division of Motor Vehicles, Disability Parking Placards Office. Apply with the New/Renew Disability Parking Placard Application. Who can certify the disability: your physician.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Mail it to RI DMV, Disability Parking Placards Office, 600 New London Avenue, Cranston, RI 02920-3024, fax it to 401-462-0829, or bring it to the Cranston headquarters, within 30 days of the physician’s certification.
constraints: A temporary (red) placard lasts 2 to 12 months.
Long-term placards last one to three years and permanent placards six years.
Veterans with a 100% service-connected disability use a separate veteran placard application.
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.phone_note: Rhode Island DMV Disability Parking Placards Office, as printed on its application form

records.name: Disability parking placard in South Carolina: how to apply
records.org: South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV)
records.description: In South Carolina, disability parking placards are issued by the South Carolina Department of Motor Vehicles (SCDMV). Apply with the Application for Placard and/or License Plate for People Who Have a Disability (RG-007A). Who can certify the disability: a licensed physician, advanced practice registered nurse or physician assistant.
records.next_step: Open the application form at the link and have the medical part completed. Apply at an SCDMV branch, or mail it with a check or money order (no cash) to SC Department of Motor Vehicles, PO Box 1498, Blythewood, SC 29016-0019.
constraints: A temporary placard is for an impairment lasting at least four months and no more than one year.
The placard fee is $1, with one placard per person. A permanent placard is valid for four years.
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.contact_how: The link opens the state’s application form (a Word document), which says where to send it.

records.name: Disability parking placard in South Dakota: how to apply
records.org: South Dakota Department of Revenue, Motor Vehicle Division (through county treasurers)
records.description: In South Dakota, disability parking placards are issued by the South Dakota Department of Revenue, Motor Vehicle Division (through county treasurers). Apply with the Disabled Person Parking Permit and License Plates Application (Form 1305). Who can certify the disability: a physician.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Fill out the form (it can be completed online, then printed), have your physician sign it, and file it with the county treasurer in the county where you live.
constraints: Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.contact_how: Apply through the agency’s page, which lists its offices and how to reach them.

records.name: Disability parking placard in Tennessee: how to apply
records.org: Tennessee Department of Revenue (through county clerks)
records.description: In Tennessee, disability parking placards are issued by the Tennessee Department of Revenue (through county clerks). Apply with the Application for Disabled Person License Plate, Placard, or Decal (RV-F1310301). Who can certify the disability: a licensed medical doctor, physician assistant or nurse practitioner, licensed chiropractic physician, licensed physical therapist, or Christian Science practitioner.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Submit the form in person or by mail to your county clerk’s office.
constraints: A temporary placard lasts up to six months and costs $10.
A permanent placard costs $26.50 (no charge if a vehicle is registered in your name) and is renewed every two years for $3. County clerks may add their own fees.
Tennessee drivers who are deaf or hard of hearing can ask their county clerk to add a deaf or hard of hearing designation to their vehicle registration that law enforcement can see.
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.contact_how: Apply through the agency’s page, which lists its offices and how to reach them.

records.name: Disability parking placard in Texas: how to apply
records.org: Texas Department of Motor Vehicles (through county tax assessor-collectors)
records.description: In Texas, disability parking placards are issued by the Texas Department of Motor Vehicles (through county tax assessor-collectors). Apply with the Application for Persons with Disabilities Parking Placard and/or License Plate (VTR-214). Who can certify the disability: a physician, podiatrist, optometrist, or qualifying physician assistant or advanced practice nurse licensed in Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana, New Mexico or Oklahoma (or practicing at a Texas military installation or VA facility); the signature must be notarized unless you attach an original prescription.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Submit it in person or by mail to the county tax assessor-collector’s office where you live (or, for a placard, where you are getting medical treatment), with a copy of your photo ID.
constraints: A permanent (blue) placard is free; a temporary (red) placard costs $5.
Vehicles showing a disability placard or plate do not pay state or local government parking meter fees; federal meters and airport parking are not covered.
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.contact_how: Apply through the agency’s page, which lists its offices and how to reach them.

records.name: Disability parking placard in Utah: how to apply
records.description: In Utah, disability parking placards are issued by the Utah Division of Motor Vehicles (DMV). Apply with the Disabled Person and Physician Disability Certification (TC-842). Who can certify the disability: a licensed physician, physician assistant, physical therapist or nurse practitioner.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Apply at a local DMV office (some offices take appointments), or mail it to Motor Vehicle Division, Mail and Correspondence, PO Box 30412, Salt Lake City, UT 84130.
constraints: Paper placards are free; a durable plastic placard costs $2.50. Permanent placards can be renewed online through the Motor Vehicle Portal.
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.phone_note: Utah DMV, as listed on its disabled person plate page (toll-free 1-800-368-8824)

records.name: Disability parking placard in Vermont: how to apply
records.description: In Vermont, disability parking placards are issued by the Vermont Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV). Apply with the Disabled Parking Placard Application (VD-120) with a Medical Evaluation Report (VS-113); temporary placards use form VL-038. Who can certify the disability: a licensed physician (on the Medical Evaluation Report).
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Send the forms to the Department of Motor Vehicles, 120 State Street, Montpelier, VT 05603.
constraints: A temporary placard lasts up to six months and cannot be renewed.
A regular permanent placard lasts four years.
A vehicle with a disability placard or plate may park free, with no time limit, in time-limited parking zones in Vermont.
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.contact_how: Apply through the agency’s page, which lists its offices and how to reach them.

records.name: Disability parking placard in Virginia: how to apply
records.description: In Virginia, disability parking placards are issued by the Virginia Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV). Apply with the Disabled Parking Placard or License Plates Application (MED 10). Who can certify the disability: a physician, physician assistant or nurse practitioner; a podiatrist or chiropractor for certain listed conditions.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Mail it to Virginia DMV, P.O. Box 85815, Richmond, VA 23285-5815, or apply at any DMV customer service center or DMV Select office. In person you get a receipt that lets you park for up to 15 days while the placard is mailed.
constraints: A temporary placard is valid for up to 12 months.
There is no fee for temporary or permanent placards. A permanent placard lasts five years and renews automatically by mail.

Virginia also issues placards for conditions that create a safety concern while walking, such as Alzheimer’s disease or blindness, and allows up to four hours free at meters and time-limited spaces unless a locality says otherwise.
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.contact_how: Apply through the agency’s page, which lists its offices and how to reach them.

records.name: Disability parking placard in Washington: how to apply
records.description: In Washington, disability parking placards are issued by the Washington State Department of Licensing (DOL). Apply with the Disabled Parking Application for Individuals, plus a separate signed prescription or authorization from your provider. Who can certify the disability: a medical doctor, osteopath, chiropractor, podiatrist, naturopath, advanced registered nurse practitioner or physician assistant.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Bring the application to a vehicle licensing office or mail it to Department of Licensing, PO Box 9043, Olympia, WA 98507. Temporary applications can also be submitted online.
constraints: A temporary (red) placard is valid for up to one year and has no fee.
Placards are free. Permanent privileges last five years and need a new prescription to renew.
Washington’s qualifying conditions include acute sensitivity to vehicle emissions and porphyria. Veterans rated 70% or higher who use a service animal can apply with a separate veteran form.
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.phone_note: DOL Customer Care, as printed on its disabled parking replacement form

records.name: Disability parking placard in West Virginia: how to apply
records.org: West Virginia Division of Motor Vehicles (DMV)
records.description: In West Virginia, disability parking placards are issued by the West Virginia Division of Motor Vehicles (DMV). Apply with the Parking Application for a Mobility Impaired Person (DMV-41-TR). Who can certify the disability: a licensed physician (MD or DO), chiropractor, advanced nurse practitioner or physician assistant.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Mail it to WV DMV, Mobility Impaired Placards & Plates, PO Box 17030, Charleston, WV 25317. Applications are also available at DMV offices and State Police detachments.
constraints: A temporary (red) placard is valid for up to six months.
A permanent (blue) placard lasts five years; renewing needs a new medical certification. A replacement placard costs $5.
People with a communication disability can ask the DMV to add them to its communication disability list (form DMV-41-CD).
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.phone_note: West Virginia DMV, as printed on its mobility impaired parking application

records.name: Disability parking placard in Wisconsin: how to apply
records.org: Wisconsin Department of Transportation, Division of Motor Vehicles (DMV)
records.description: In Wisconsin, disability parking placards are issued by the Wisconsin Department of Transportation, Division of Motor Vehicles (DMV). Apply with the Permanent Disabled Parking Identification Permit Application (MV2548); temporary permits use form MV2933. Who can certify the disability: an authorized health care specialist, who can also certify online.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Apply at a DMV customer service center that lists "disabled parking ID cards" among its services.
constraints: A temporary (red) permit is issued for up to six months.
A permanent (blue) permit is issued for four years and needs a new certification to renew.

Permit holders may park without paying at meters, and without the time limit, in spaces with limits of half an hour or more on municipal lots and streets. Wisconsin DMV also has an Invisible Disability Disclosure form (MV2167).
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.contact_how: Apply through the agency’s page, which lists its offices and how to reach them.

records.name: Disability parking placard in Wyoming: how to apply
records.org: Wyoming Department of Transportation (WYDOT), Driver Services
records.description: In Wyoming, disability parking placards are issued by the Wyoming Department of Transportation (WYDOT), Driver Services. Apply with the Application for Disabled Parking Identification Placard. Who can certify the disability: a physician or advanced practice registered nurse.
records.next_step: Open the agency’s page for the current form and have the medical part completed. Apply online through oneWYO, or mail the form to WYDOT Driver Services, Driver Review, 5300 Bishop Blvd., Cheyenne, WY 82009-3340. The placard is mailed to you.
constraints: A temporary placard is valid for up to six months and can be renewed once.
There is no fee for placards.
Wyoming’s qualifying conditions include a severe vision or hearing impairment that limits mobility.
Forms, fees and rules change. Check the agency’s page before you apply.
records.phone_note: WYDOT Driver Services, as printed on its placard application

records.name: ALS Association Care Services: information, referral and local care teams
records.description: The ALS Association’s Care Services line gives general, non-medical information and referrals to people living with ALS and their families. The Association says its care programs are free of charge and include local care teams, support groups and a network of certified ALS centers and clinics.
records.next_step: Call and ask to be connected with the care team that serves your area. Ask about support groups and the certified ALS clinic nearest you.
constraints: Care Services gives general information, not medical advice.
For questions about disability benefits or health insurance, the ALS Insurance and Benefits Resource Line, run with Patient Advocate Foundation, offers free case management at 1-844-244-1306.
records.phone_note: Care Services line, as listed on the Association’s contact page

records.name: Arthritis Foundation Helpline
records.description: A free helpline for people with arthritis and their families. Helpline staff answer questions by phone or web chat and point callers to resources, including the Foundation’s Connect Groups for peer support. A Spanish-speaking staff member is available.
records.next_step: Call or start a web chat and say what you need help with. Ask about Connect Groups near you or online.
constraints: Open Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern.
Helpline staff are not medically trained and do not give medical advice.
If you leave a message, expect a call back within two business days.
records.phone_note: Arthritis Foundation Helpline

records.name: Spina Bifida Association National Resource Center
records.description: The National Resource Center answers questions from people with spina bifida and their families, in English and Spanish. Staff can refer callers to spina bifida clinics, local services and support. The Association also offers peer mentors for families.
records.next_step: Call and ask for extension 800. Say where you live and what you need, such as a clinic, local services or a family to talk with.
constraints: Clinics and local services differ from place to place.
records.phone_note: Ask for extension 800, the National Resource Center

records.name: Sickle Cell Disease Association of America: find a member organization near you
records.org: Sickle Cell Disease Association of America
records.description: The national association for people living with sickle cell disease. Its website has a finder for member organizations, community groups in many states that offer local services and support.
records.next_step: Use the member organization finder to locate the group nearest you, or call the national office and ask who serves your area. Ask about support groups.
constraints: Member organizations are in some states, not all, and their services differ.
records.phone_note: National office, as listed on the association’s website

records.name: National Down Syndrome Society Helpline
records.description: A toll-free helpline for people with Down syndrome and their families. NDSS can refer families to its network of more than 350 local parent support groups and to Down syndrome clinics.
records.next_step: Call or email and ask for the parent support group and the Down syndrome clinic closest to you.
constraints: Open Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern.
records.phone_note: NDSS Helpline, toll-free

records.name: NORD: help for people living with a rare disease
records.description: NORD’s helpline helps people with rare diseases and their families find specialists and resources. NORD also runs RareCare patient assistance programs, which can help eligible patients with medication costs, insurance premiums and copays, and emergency needs, and a respite program for caregivers.
records.next_step: Call and describe the diagnosis and what you need. Ask whether a RareCare assistance program is open for your condition.
constraints: Open Monday to Thursday, 8:30 a.m. to 7 p.m., and Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern.
Assistance programs are open to U.S. citizens and permanent residents, and each has its own eligibility rules.
records.phone_note: NORD helpline; en español (844) 259-7178

records.name: CF Foundation Compass: free help with insurance, money and legal questions for people with cystic fibrosis
records.description: Compass is a free, confidential service from the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation. Case managers work one on one with people with cystic fibrosis and their families on health insurance, finances, legal information and Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI). Spanish-speaking case managers are available.
records.next_step: Call 844-COMPASS or email, and describe the problem, such as an insurance denial or a disability application.
constraints: Compass does not give money, legal advice or clinical information.
Email and online requests can take three to five business days to answer.
records.phone_note: 844-COMPASS

records.name: United Cerebral Palsy: find programs in your area
records.description: UCP runs an information and referral service that helps people find programs in their area, including those of UCP’s network of local affiliates.
records.next_step: Call the information and referral line and ask which programs and which UCP affiliate serve where you live.
constraints: What is available depends on where you live.
records.phone_note: Information and referral line; UCP national office (800) 872-5827

records.name: Little People of America: support for people with dwarfism and their families
records.description: A national organization for people of short stature and their families. Its national office can connect you with local contacts and with a network of parents and peers across the country. LPA also offers some financial help, such as scholarships and medical assistance funds, to people who qualify.
records.next_step: Call the national office and ask for the local contacts and the parent or peer support in your area.
constraints: Some services, such as consultations with doctors on LPA’s Medical Advisory Board, are membership benefits, and membership has annual dues.
records.phone_note: 1-888-LPA-2001. LPA says the line is available 24 hours a day

records.name: GBS|CIDP Foundation International: patient services and local liaisons
records.description: The Foundation supports people with Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) and related conditions, and their caregivers. Its Patient Services team takes calls, and the Foundation lists Centers of Excellence, local chapters and volunteer liaisons, and arranges visits from people who have recovered.
records.next_step: Call Patient Services and ask for the chapter or liaison near you and the closest Center of Excellence.
constraints: Chapters and liaisons are volunteers, so what is offered differs by area.
records.phone_note: Toll-free; direct line (610) 667-0131

records.name: Huntington’s Disease Society of America Helpline
records.description: A helpline for families affected by Huntington’s disease, staffed by trained social workers. HDSA also has social workers who help families find community services in their region, and Centers of Excellence for Huntington’s disease care.
records.next_step: Call the helpline and ask for the HDSA social worker who covers your area and the nearest Center of Excellence.
constraints: Open Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern.

records.name: Depression and Bipolar Support Alliance: free peer support groups
records.description: DBSA runs free support groups, led by peers, for people living with depression or bipolar disorder. Groups meet in person through local chapters and online. There are also groups for family and friends, for parents and caregivers, and for particular communities.
records.next_step: Open DBSA’s support page, choose an in-person or online group, and sign up. Online groups ask you to register, at no charge.
constraints: Support groups are not group therapy.
In a crisis, call or text 988.
records.contact_how: Find a group on DBSA’s support page.

records.name: Cure SMA: community support for spinal muscular atrophy
records.description: Cure SMA’s community support staff help people with spinal muscular atrophy and their families with information, connections to local resources and someone to listen. Programs include information packets, care packages for newly diagnosed families, support packages for teens and adults, an equipment loan pool, local chapters and grief support.
records.next_step: Call or email and ask for a member of the community support staff. If you need equipment, ask about the loan pool.
constraints: Loan equipment depends on what has been donated, so you may be put on a waiting list.
records.phone_note: Cure SMA national office

records.name: Charcot-Marie-Tooth Association: questions and local branches
records.description: The CMTA serves people with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT) and their families. It answers general questions by phone and email, and its branches are volunteer-led local support groups where people with CMT share resources and experiences.
records.next_step: Call or email with your question, or find the CMTA branch nearest you on the website.
constraints: The toll-free number works in the U.S. only.

records.name: Post-Polio Health International: support groups and clinics for polio survivors and home ventilator users
records.org: Post-Polio Health International (including International Ventilator Users Network)
records.description: A national organization that gathers and shares information for polio survivors and people who use home ventilators, their caregivers and families. Its yearly Post-Polio Directory lists support groups and health professionals state by state.
records.next_step: Open the current Post-Polio Directory to find a support group or clinic in your state, or write or call the office. Include your name and mailing address.
constraints: The office keeps limited weekday hours.
records.phone_note: Office line, as listed on the organization’s contact page and directory

records.name: Hydrocephalus Association Helpline
records.description: A toll-free helpline where staff answer questions about hydrocephalus and refer callers to educational resources and support programs. The Association also offers HydrocephalusCONNECT, one-to-one support from trained volunteers who live with hydrocephalus or care for someone who does, and Community Networks, its support groups, including a Spanish-speaking group and a network for U.S. military members and families.
records.next_step: Call or email. If no one answers, leave your name, phone number, the best time to call and your time zone.
constraints: Open Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern.
Messages are returned within 24 to 48 hours.
records.phone_note: Hydrocephalus Association Helpline

records.name: Osteogenesis Imperfecta Foundation: questions, clinics and support networks
records.description: The OI Foundation answers questions from people with osteogenesis imperfecta, a genetic condition in which bones break easily, and from their families. It keeps a directory of OI clinics, lists support networks and can tell families about doctors near them who have treated OI.
records.next_step: Call or email the Foundation, or open the OI Clinic Directory on its website to find a clinic near you.
constraints: The office is open Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern.
records.phone_note: Toll-free; main line (301) 947-0083

records.name: National Ataxia Foundation: support groups and questions
records.description: NAF serves people with ataxia and their families. It lists U.S. support groups by state, virtual groups, and groups for particular communities, including African Americans with ataxia, parents with ataxia, Spanish speakers and military members.
records.next_step: Open the support group page and choose your state, or call or email NAF with general questions.
constraints: Support groups are led by volunteers; contact details are on each group’s listing.
records.phone_note: NAF general questions

records.name: American Cancer Society 24/7 cancer helpline
records.description: Trained cancer helpline specialists answer questions about cancer and connect callers with American Cancer Society programs and other resources, any time of day or night. Programs include free rides to treatment in some communities and free Hope Lodge lodging when treatment is far from home.
records.next_step: Call at any hour and say what you need, such as information about a diagnosis, a ride to treatment or a place to stay during treatment.
constraints: Rides and lodging are not available everywhere.
Live chat on the website is available on weekdays.
records.phone_note: Available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week

records.name: Road To Recovery: free rides to cancer treatment
records.description: In some communities, American Cancer Society volunteer drivers give free rides to cancer-related medical appointments for patients who have no way to get there. Drivers pick you up, take you to your appointment and bring you home.
records.next_step: Call the American Cancer Society several business days before your appointment and ask whether Road To Recovery drivers serve your area.
constraints: Rides are only for cancer-related appointments.
A caregiver may need to come along if the patient cannot walk without help or is under 18.
It can take several business days to arrange a ride.
records.phone_note: American Cancer Society, 24 hours a day

records.name: American Lung Association Lung HelpLine
records.description: A free helpline staffed by registered nurses, respiratory therapists and tobacco treatment specialists. They answer questions about lung disease, including COPD, asthma and lung cancer, and can help you find pulmonary rehabilitation programs near you. Spanish-speaking staff and a translation service are available.
records.next_step: Call 1-800-LUNGUSA or send a question online, and ask about pulmonary rehabilitation and support near you.
constraints: The Lung HelpLine is open seven days a week. Questions sent online are answered by email.
records.phone_note: 1-800-LUNGUSA

records.name: NKF Cares: help line for kidney disease, dialysis and transplant
records.description: A free help line for patients, family members and care partners affected by kidney disease, organ donation or transplantation. Trained specialists answer questions in English and Spanish. The Foundation also offers NKF Peers, free mentoring by phone from people who have been through dialysis, transplant or living donation.
records.next_step: Call or email and say what you need, such as help understanding treatment choices or going back to work. Ask about NKF Peers.
constraints: Open Monday to Friday, 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. Eastern.
records.phone_note: 855-NKF-CARES

records.name: National Resource Center on ADHD helpline (CHADD)
records.org: CHADD (Children and Adults with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder)
records.description: CHADD’s National Resource Center on ADHD runs a helpline where health information specialists answer questions about ADHD in children and adults, in English and Spanish. CHADD also has local chapters and support groups and an online directory of professionals.
records.next_step: Call on a weekday afternoon and ask how to find an ADHD evaluation, treatment or a support group near you.
constraints: Open Monday to Friday, 1 to 5 p.m. Eastern.
The center does not give counseling, medical or legal advice and does not refer you to a specific professional, but it can help you choose one.
records.phone_note: ADHD helpline; hablamos español

records.name: Tourette Association of America: local support and Centers of Excellence
records.description: The national organization for people with Tourette syndrome and other tic disorders, and their families. Its website lists chapters, support groups and Centers of Excellence state by state, and staff answer questions by email, chat and phone.
records.next_step: Find your state on the local support page, or contact the Association and ask what support is near you.
constraints: If your state is not listed, the Association can still suggest the nearest support.
In a mental health crisis, call or text 988.
records.phone_note: 888-4-TOURET

records.name: Lupus Foundation of America: ask a health educator
records.description: Health education specialists give free, non-medical support, information about lupus and help finding resources, in English and Spanish. The Foundation and its partners also run lupus support groups across the country.
records.next_step: Call and leave your question, and a health education specialist will call you back. You can also use the online form.
constraints: Health educators give non-medical support, not medical advice.
records.phone_note: A health education specialist calls you back

records.name: Supported decision-making: an alternative to guardianship
records.org: National Resource Center for Supported Decision-Making
records.description: Supported decision-making lets a person with a disability use trusted friends, family members and professionals to help them understand choices and make their own decisions. The National Resource Center describes it as a less restrictive alternative to guardianship and has a page for each state with its laws and contacts.
records.next_step: Open the center’s page for your state before anyone files for guardianship. Ask whether a supported decision-making agreement, a power of attorney, an advance directive or a health care proxy would meet the need.
constraints: Laws on supported decision-making differ from state to state.
The center gives information, not legal advice. For legal help, contact your state’s Protection and Advocacy agency or legal aid.
records.contact_how: Find your state on the center’s website.

records.name: Donated Dental Services: free dental care from volunteer dentists
records.description: Dental Lifeline Network’s Donated Dental Services program arranges free, comprehensive dental treatment from volunteer dentists and dental labs. It is for people who cannot afford care and who are 65 or older, have a permanent disability, or need dental care for a medical reason.
records.next_step: Open your state’s page from the Dental Lifeline Network help page and apply. If you are under 65, have your Social Security disability award letter ready.
constraints: You must use any dental coverage you have first, including Medicaid.
There is a waiting list, and some areas are closed to new applications.
Emergency and cosmetic care are not provided, and the program helps each person once.
records.contact_how: Apply through your state’s page on the Dental Lifeline Network site.

records.name: Assistance Dogs International: find an accredited service dog program
records.description: ADI accredits nonprofit programs that train assistance dogs. Its member search lists accredited programs by area and shows which ones work with veterans or will consider working with a person’s own dog. ADI itself does not provide, train or certify dogs.
records.next_step: Use the member search to find accredited programs that serve your area, then ask each program about its waiting list, fees and requirements.
constraints: Each program sets its own fees; many charge little or nothing.
Veterans: VA’s service dog benefit requires a dog trained by an ADI- or IGDF-accredited program.
records.contact_how: Search for accredited programs on the ADI website.

records.name: Independent living help for older adults with vision loss in Alabama
records.org: Alabama Department of Rehabilitation Services (OASIS program)
records.description: This is Alabama’s program under the federal Independent Living Services for Older Individuals who are Blind (OIB) grant, run by the Alabama Department of Rehabilitation Services (OASIS program). According to Time To Be Bold, these services often include training in making the most of remaining vision, using magnifiers and other devices, using phones and computers, staying safe and organized at home and getting around the community. Who qualifies, according to the state page: Alabamians 55 and older with a significant visual impairment that affects at least one daily activity. Staff confirm this with an assessment, usually at home.
records.next_step: Call to be put on the referral list for your area. Anyone can make the referral, including you, a relative or your eye doctor. No paperwork is needed to start, though medical records help.
constraints: The state page lists 11 local OASIS offices.
Under the federal program these services are meant for people 55 and older who are not looking for work. If you want to keep or find a job, ask about vocational rehabilitation instead.
If there is a waiting list, Time To Be Bold suggests Hadley’s free lessons on living with vision loss, by phone, mail or online: 800-323-4238.
records.phone_note: Main office line as listed on Time To Be Bold; also 205-290-4400

If there is a waiting list, Time To Be Bold suggests Hadley’s free lessons on living with vision loss, by phone, mail or online: 800-323-4238.
records.contact_how: Contact details are on the agency page linked here. The agency’s main line is also in this directory.

records.name: Independent living help for older adults with vision loss in West Virginia
records.org: West Virginia Division of Rehabilitation Services (VISIONS program)
records.description: VISIONS (Visually Impaired Seniors In-Home Outreach and Networking Services) is a free West Virginia program for people 55 and older who are not working and have a permanent visual impairment that affects daily living. Services take place at home or at a senior center or church.
records.next_step: Contact the West Virginia Division of Rehabilitation Services and ask about VISIONS.
constraints: Under the federal program these services are meant for people 55 and older who are not looking for work. If you want to keep or find a job, ask about vocational rehabilitation instead.
If there is a waiting list, Time To Be Bold suggests Hadley’s free lessons on living with vision loss, by phone, mail or online: 800-323-4238.
records.contact_how: Contact details are on the agency page linked here. The agency’s main line is also in this directory.

records.name: National Federation of the Blind: state affiliates and local chapters
records.description: The National Federation of the Blind is an organization of blind people, families with blind children, people with low vision or vision loss, and deafblind people. It has an affiliate in every state, D.C. and Puerto Rico, with local chapters and, in many states, divisions for groups such as students, parents and seniors. Affiliates can tell you about local chapters and meetings, programs, resources, libraries for the blind and state conventions.
records.next_step: Find your state on the NFB’s affiliates page and contact the affiliate, or call the national office.
constraints: The NFB is a membership organization, not a government agency; for rehabilitation services, contact your state’s agency for the blind.
records.phone_note: National headquarters in Baltimore, as listed on the NFB contact page

records.name: NFB-NEWSLINE: free audio newspapers and magazines
records.description: NFB-NEWSLINE is a free audio news service with more than 500 publications, emergency weather alerts, job listings and more. Anyone who cannot read printed publications because of vision loss, dyslexia or a physical disability can sign up.
records.next_step: Call your state’s library for the blind and print-disabled, or the NFB, to ask for an application. You can also apply online or by mail.
constraints: Some states add their own local newspapers; ask your state library what is carried where you live.
records.phone_note: NFB-NEWSLINE sign-up line, as listed on the NFB’s page

records.name: National Scleroderma Foundation HOPE Line
records.description: The HOPE Line is a free service for people living with scleroderma, caregivers, families and the public. The foundation can also connect you with its chapters and more than 100 support groups, and help you find designated scleroderma centers and specialists.
records.next_step: Call the HOPE Line or email the foundation. After hours, leave a voicemail.
constraints: The line is answered 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern. The foundation says every inquiry gets a response within two business days.
records.phone_note: 800-722-HOPE, as listed on the foundation’s contact page

records.name: TSC Alliance Support Navigators (tuberous sclerosis complex)
records.description: The TSC Alliance’s Support Navigators answer questions about tuberous sclerosis complex, help you understand a diagnosis, help find TSC specialists, talk through treatment options and give emotional support and connections to others with TSC.
records.next_step: Call the support line or email the navigators.
constraints: The support line is answered 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. Eastern. In a medical emergency, call 911.
records.phone_note: Support line, as listed on the alliance’s page

records.name: Crohn’s & Colitis Foundation IBD Help Center
records.description: Information specialists at the IBD Help Center answer questions about Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis and give guidance and support, including for people facing financial hardship, unstable housing or limited access to health care. Help is available in more than 170 languages, including Spanish. The foundation also runs support groups and Power of Two, which matches you by phone with another patient or caregiver.
records.next_step: Call and speak with a specialist or leave a message at any time, or use the live chat on the help center page.
constraints: For Power of Two, call the same number and press extension 8.
records.phone_note: 888-MY-GUT-PAIN, as listed on the foundation’s help center page

records.name: Friedreich’s Ataxia Research Alliance (FARA): help after a diagnosis
records.description: FARA has guides for adults newly diagnosed with Friedreich’s ataxia and for parents of a child with a new diagnosis, and can connect you with others in the FA community, including its Ambassador Program of people living with FA and a free email support group for parents of children with FA or other childhood-onset ataxias.
records.next_step: Call or email FARA with your questions, or use the form on its newly diagnosed page to be connected with someone.
records.phone_note: As listed on FARA’s contact page

records.name: The Ehlers-Danlos Society: support group directory
records.description: The society keeps a directory of support groups and charities for Ehlers-Danlos syndromes, hypermobility spectrum disorders and related conditions, including local and online groups across the United States. It also has a U.S. resource page on benefits, housing, food help and crisis support.
records.next_step: Open the directory and look for a group in your area or one that meets online, then contact the group directly.
constraints: The groups in the directory are run separately from the society; check each group’s details with the group.
records.contact_how: Contact details for each group are in the society’s directory.

records.name: American Diabetes Association Center for Information (1-800-DIABETES)
records.description: Information specialists at the American Diabetes Association answer questions by phone, chat and email for people with diabetes and their caregivers. Through its Safe at School program, the association also helps families with questions about a child’s rights and problems with diabetes care at school.
records.next_step: Call 1-800-DIABETES and say what you need, such as information, help with a school problem, or a diabetes information packet.
records.phone_note: 1-800-DIABETES, as listed on the association’s page

records.name: ASHA ProFind: find a speech-language pathologist or audiologist
records.description: ASHA ProFind lists more than 20,000 ASHA-certified audiologists and speech-language pathologists who are accepting referrals. Speech-language pathologists help with speech, language, stuttering, voice and swallowing problems, including after a stroke; audiologists help with hearing.
records.next_step: Search ProFind by location for an audiologist or a speech-language pathologist. You can also ask your doctor or your local school.
constraints: Look for CCC-SLP or CCC-A after a provider’s name; it means ASHA certification.
records.phone_note: ASHA, Monday to Friday 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern, as listed on ASHA’s site

records.name: Stuttering Foundation: referral lists of stuttering specialists
records.description: The Stuttering Foundation keeps referral lists of speech-language pathologists who specialize in stuttering, in the United States and other countries, along with intensive and summer clinics.
records.next_step: Open the referral list and look for a specialist near you. If there is none nearby, the foundation suggests a local university, hospital, or speech and hearing clinic.
records.contact_how: Specialists’ contact details are on the foundation’s referral lists.

records.name: Learning Disabilities Association of America: state affiliates
records.description: LDA is a national network of people with learning disabilities, their families and the professionals who work with them. Its 38 state affiliates may offer support groups, information meetings, resource libraries, advocacy help, newsletters and conferences.
records.next_step: Choose your state on LDA’s affiliates page and contact the affiliate.
constraints: Not every state has an affiliate.
records.contact_how: Choose your state on the affiliates page.

records.name: Mental Health America: find a peer-run warmline
records.description: A warmline is a peer-run listening line answered by people in recovery themselves. It is for when you are not in crisis but want to talk to someone. Mental Health America lists warmlines by state.
records.next_step: Use MHA’s warmline finder to see whether your state has one.
constraints: If you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988, or text MHA to 741741.
records.contact_how: Use the warmline finder on MHA’s contact page.

records.name: Independent living help for older adults with vision loss in South Dakota
records.org: South Dakota Division of Service to the Blind and Visually Impaired
records.description: South Dakota’s Division of Service to the Blind and Visually Impaired works with blind and visually impaired people on employment and independent living. The state board’s 2025 annual report describes its Independent Living Program and expanded outreach to older adults adjusting to vision changes.
records.next_step: Contact the division and ask about independent living services for older adults with vision loss.
constraints: The report does not set out who qualifies; ask when you contact the division. If you want to keep or find a job, ask about vocational rehabilitation instead.
If there is a waiting list, Time To Be Bold suggests Hadley’s free lessons on living with vision loss, by phone, mail or online: 800-323-4238.
records.contact_how: Contact details are on the agency page linked here. The agency’s main line is also in this directory.

records.name: Alabama Department of Rehabilitation Services: Deaf and Hard of Hearing Services
records.org: State program for people who are deaf or hard of hearing
records.description: The national roster of state agencies lists none for Alabama. Deaf and Hard of Hearing Services is one of four programs in the Alabama Department of Rehabilitation Services’ Blind and Deaf program, which serves Alabamians statewide.
records.next_step: Contact the agency using the phone, videophone or email shown here, and say what you need, such as an interpreter or captioner, phone equipment, advocacy or help for your family. Ask who to contact if the agency does not offer it.
constraints: TTY users can dial 711.
What these agencies do differs from state to state. Some provide services directly; others advise the state.
records.phone_note: For deaf, hard of hearing, or blind and deaf services, as listed on the department’s page; main line 334-293-7500

records.name: North Dakota School for the Deaf / Resource Center for Deaf and Hard of Hearing
records.org: State program for people who are deaf or hard of hearing
records.description: The national roster of state agencies lists none for North Dakota. The state School for the Deaf also runs a resource center whose adult services are open to every North Dakotan who is deaf or hard of hearing, whatever their age or the cause of the hearing loss, including older adults losing hearing with age. It has outreach offices around the state.
records.next_step: Contact the agency using the phone, videophone or email shown here, and say what you need, such as an interpreter or captioner, phone equipment, advocacy or help for your family. Ask who to contact if the agency does not offer it.
constraints: What these agencies do differs from state to state. Some provide services directly; others advise the state.
records.phone_note: Voice and TTY, as listed on the school’s contact page; videophone 701-581-3059; toll-free in North Dakota 800-887-2980 (state CareChoice listing)

records.name: South Dakota Division of Rehabilitation Services: interpreter help for deaf and hard of hearing people
records.org: State program for people who are deaf or hard of hearing
records.description: The national roster of state agencies lists none for South Dakota. The state Division of Rehabilitation Services keeps the South Dakota Interpreter Registry and runs a program that can help pay for sign language interpreters in situations the Americans with Disabilities Act does not cover, such as events held by nonprofits, faith groups or youth organizations.
records.next_step: Look up interpreters on the state registry, or contact the division to ask about help paying for one.
constraints: The interpreter payment program does not cover job situations.
What these agencies do differs from state to state. Some provide services directly; others advise the state.
records.phone_note: As listed on the division’s interpreter page

records.name: Wyoming Adult Hearing Aid Program
records.description: A state-funded program for adults with hearing loss, created by state law. Subject to available funding, it covers up to one hearing aid per ear, hearing aid insurance for loss or damage, a fitting and an initial set of ear molds.
records.next_step: Read the program’s FAQ for who qualifies and how to apply.
constraints: The program does not cover hearing tests.
Coverage depends on state funding being available.
records.contact_how: How to apply is explained in the program’s FAQ, linked here.

records.name: NMEDA dealer locator: wheelchair accessible vehicles and adaptive driving equipment
records.description: NMEDA, the trade association of mobility equipment dealers in the United States and Canada, runs a locator for dealers accredited under its Quality Assurance Program (QAP), which sell, install and service wheelchair accessible vehicles and adaptive driving equipment. NMEDA also publishes a consumer buying guide that walks through vehicle conversions and adaptive equipment.
records.next_step: Use the dealer locator to find a QAP-accredited dealer near you, and read the buying guide before you shop.
constraints: The locator page, as read, asks for your name, email and phone so dealers can contact you. NMEDA is a dealers’ association, so expect sales contact.

Mobility Talk receives nothing from NMEDA or any dealer.
records.contact_how: Use the dealer locator on NMEDA’s site.

records.name: Independent living help for older adults with vision loss in Guam
records.description: Guam’s Division of Vocational Rehabilitation administers Guam’s plan for Independent Living for the Older Blind, the federal program for people 55 and older with vision loss.
records.next_step: Call the department and ask about independent living services for older adults who are blind or have low vision.
constraints: Under the federal program these services are meant for people 55 and older who are not looking for work. If you want to keep or find a job, ask about vocational rehabilitation instead.
